X beg to move the following amendment:
That all the words after the word 'That' to the end of the question be left out and the following substituted therefor :-' the Bill be referred back to a Committee of the Whole House with power to amend the same as follows :-
Should the government be of opinion that at any time during the continuance of any obligation of the government In respect of the western division, or during the said lease of the eastern division, that the earnings upon the traffic interchanged between the Gran 1 Trunk Pacific Railway Company's system of railways and the system of railways of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, have not been properly apportioned between the said two companies, the question of such apportionment shall be determined by arbitrators to be appointed by the government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada in like manner as is proviaed with regard to arbitrators by paragraph 47 of the said agreement, or he determined by the board of railway commissioners as mentioned in section 19 of the said agreement. And the government shall have the right to inspect all books of account, statements, contracts, correspondence, vouchers, waybills and all other papers and documents of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, the inspection of which may he considered necessary for the purpose of investigating or determinyig any question, matter or thing arising out of the said agreement, or the said lease or the provisions of this Act, or connected with the obligations or undertakings of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company entered into pursuant to the said agreement, or. lease, or to this Act.
The object of this amendment is to enlarge the scope of section 19 of the agreement. The government in that section endeavours to protect itself against a possible unfair division of the earnings on the' Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company will own the western division of the line and it will be lessee of the eastern 'division. Its liability in certain years to pay rent upon the eastern division depends, under the contract, upon whether there shall foe net earnings in those years. It might, therefore, be to the interests of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to so divide the earnings as between the western division and the eastern division of the railway that all its profits would go to its own property, the western division, and that there should be no net earnings upon the eastern division, and thereby the company would escape, in certain years, any liability to pay rent. The government very properly saw that this might arise, and, under section 19, they protected themselves fairly enough against it. The provision of that section is :
' "t

The company shall keep separate accounts of the earnings and expenditure of the eastern and western divisions, and, for the purposes of this agreement, the earnings from through traffic shall be apportioned between the eastern and western divisions, according to the usual practice of connecting lines of railway operated by two separate companies ;

Then it goes on to provide that, in case of a dispute between the government and the railway company in that regard the matter shall be left to arbitration, or, in the event of a board of railway commissioners being appointed, the board of commissioners shall deal with the dispute as between the company and the government. All that is fair and reasonable and would be expected in such a case as this. But the government seem entirely to overlook the very important consideration that the very thing they are protecting themselves against as to the western and eastern divisions of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, may occur as between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway. A very important portion of the through-traffic will pass over both the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway, and there will be through-earnings on that traffic to be divided and apportioned between the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk. Now the Grand Trunk, it is quite clear, will control both systems, and it will be quite possible for that company, by taking too large a proportion of the through-earnings to itself in respect of its own railway, so to lessen the earnings upon the Grand Trunk Pacific that they will accomplish the very object tha't the government in this section 19 have endeavoured to prevent. Therefore I propose by this amendment to provide that wherever there may be a question as to whether the Grand Trunk is taking to itself, for its own railway, a larger proportion of the through-earnings than it ought to take, the government can intervene, and if the parties cannot agree, can ask that the matter shall be referred to arbitration, so that the Grand Trunk Pacific shall get its due share of the earnings, and that in consequence the government will be certain to get its rent. The Minister of Finance the other day seemed to think that the government was sufficiently protected because the Board of Railway Commissioners might intervene. But that is really a mistake ; there can be no question about that. The Board of Railway Commissioners can only intervene to settle questions where two railway companies differ about a division of their through-rates. But there will be no such difference here, there is no possibility of a difference between the Grand Trunk Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. No one will ever hear of a dispute between these two companies as to the apportionment of the earnings, and unless there is some dispute, the Board of , Commissioners cannot intervene. They can, 400	'	'
however intervene if it is made part of the bargain between the government and the companies; while if we are left to the statutory provision that the Board of Railway Commissioners can settle disputes between two railway companies as to the apportionment of through-traffic, such a dispute will never arise. Therefore it is that I move this resolution, which I will not take up further time in discussing, because the proposition seems to be perfectly plain. The government have shown by their own agreement that they contemplate the possibility of an unfair division between the eastern and the western sections; that unfair division could only take place for the purpose of avoiding the payment of rent, and having provided against such an emergency, the government is bound to go further and prevent the same trouble arising from an unfair division between the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.

cuse is necessary for offering another amendment to this Bill. When we consider the very large sum of money that is involved in this Bill I do not think it is necessary to offer any apology for the amendment which I propose to place in your hands. Never during the history of Canada has any question of so far reaching importance been brought before the attention of this parliament, not even the Canadian Pacific Railway, as the question now under consideration in this Bill. Consequently the greatest care should be exercised by the government in dealing with the moneys to be expended on this undertaking, and every safeguard should be adopted to secure the proper and legal expenditure of every dollar of the money.
Let us look for one moment at the authority on which the money is to be expended. When work is done or a service performed it has to receive the approval of the commissioners appointed under this Act. Then, on the approval of the commissioners, certified by the chairman of the board, the Minister of Railways and Canals recommends to the bon. Minister of Finance that payments be made and payments are consequently made from time to time on the recommendation of that minister. First parliament appropriates the money by a vote, then the commissioners approve of the work and of the services performed, the Minister of Railways and Canals recommends to the lion. Minister of Finance payment and payment is made accordingly, but it is made without any audit of these accounts by any officer of this parliament until after these moneys have all been expended. The commissioners, we understand, will be appointees of the government. The Minister of Railways and Canals is a member of the government and so also is the hon. Minister of Finance. But who is to guard the rights of the people of this" country-!1 Who will represent the people in this vast expenditure of the $100,000,000 or $150,000,000 ? Even if the cost of the railway does not exceed $125,000,000, if the work is continued over five years it will result in the expenditure of $25,000,000 per annum. And yet this work under the Bill is to go on from day to day without any audit of it, such as is necessary for the protection of the people, being made. I am aware that under section 31 of the Act it is proposed that an examination and audit shall take place, but, I desire to remind the House that this examination and audit does not take place until after the money has been paid and consequently will prove to be of very little value or importance indeed. I suppose it is scarcely necessary at this stage of the question to repeat all the arguments that might be advanced against the Grand Trunk Pacific project and I shall not even attempt to repeat the majority of them. There is, however, one feature in the Bill which is of great importance to the people and parliament of Canada and particularly to the people of eastern Canada, that is, that it should be so carried out as to realize for that part of Canada all the benefits which I understand, the right hon. the leader of the government and his colleagues anticipate from its completion and operation. In order that that may be accomplished it is necessary, in the opinion of some persons who are not quite so sanguine in their hopes in respect to this matter as some others are, that the parties who are entering into the contract with the government to build and operate this road should be so bound and held that they would faithfully operate it and thereby realize all the advantages that in the course of time may be expected to result from its operation. It has been shown very clearly in the course of the discussion that the real party of the second part is the Grand Trunk Railway and it has been just as clearly brought out that the Grand Trunk Railway is not a contracting party in the ordinary sense of the word. Nor is it our opinion that they are held and bound to the fulfillment of all the agreements in the contract, or under any penalty whatever if they fail to execute these contracts. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has undertaken to secure certain action on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company but it would apparently be better if the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself were held and bound by the contract. In the opinion of hon. members upon this side of the House the contract is secured by a very slender provision

so far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company is concerned. It is admitted that the financing of the new corporation is to he largely the work of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, still it is held that there is not sufficient strength in the contract so far as the Grand Trunk Railway Company is concerned to ensure that that company may not at some time refuse to carry out its part of the contract and that the penalty which may be exacted under the terms of the contract would not be of sufficient strength or weight to prevent that company from forfeiting, from violating its agreement and refusing to carry out what they had undertaken. Therefore, with a view to improving the condition of affairs in that regard I am about to offer an amendment to the House and to ask the government to adopt it, or at least,to endeavour to secure the assent of the House to the proposition that there should be some further security than that which is contemplated in the agreement as we understand it. The only security which the government have is a claim upon $5,000,000 worth of rolling stock, a property which in the course of time must depreciate very rapidly so that its value will diminish to a point far below $5,000,000. It is quite easy to realize and to understand that the moment may come, and may come perhaps in the not very far distant future, when the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which is really the contracting party, would consider it a good business operation to forfeit and abandon that.property which is held as security for the fulfilment of this agreement. We believe that the government of the country should have some further hold upon the contracting company in order to secure that the operation of this road be continued, and that it be not thrown back to us, as it may be, In a depreciated condition. Therefore, with the view of trying to improve the security held by the country, and to furnish a much stronger guarantee that this road should be operated, and that whatever good results from its operation by the Grand Trunk Pacific as represented therein by the Grand Trunk Company, shall be more fully and more thoroughly ensured to the people of this country ; I move, seconded by Mr. Kemp, the following, as an additional clause to the Bill.
The railway and the property and equipment . of the said western division, and the equipment of the eastern division shall be charged, subject only to the mortgage obligations in the said agreement mentioned, with the payment of all rents that may become payable to the government under the said lease of the eastern division to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and with the payment of all claims of the government against the said company under any and every covenant or obligation or condition of the said lease and agreement, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company shall enter into and make all proper and sufficient mortgages, agreements and covenants with the government for that purpose.

Before fore you put the motion, Mr. Speaker, I desire to draw attention to the fact that on the second reading of this Bill, I raised a point of order as to the irregularity of the course pursued by the government in introducing the Bill. I drew attention to the fact that the Bill had reached its second reading, and although it was a Bill which involved a charge on the revenue of the country, it was not introduced by resolution, as it should be, nor had the announcement been made in the House that the consent of the Crown had been given to the Bill before its introduction. You then intimated, Mr. Speaker, that you would give your decision later on. In the meantime I presume that you have had an opportunity to consider the question, and I would like to have your ruling on it now.

I have prepared my opinion on the question whch was raised by the bon. gentleman, not on the second reading, but on the first reading. That, however, does not make a great deal of difference. This is my opinion :
A point of order has been raised as to the propriety of proceeding with Bill (No. 235) ' An Act to provide for the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway,' because that measure has not been previously considered in a Committee of the Whole, and has not been recommended by the Crown. That question is a very important one, as I had occasion to state when it was raised on motion for leave.
The rules which govern the case are Rules 80 and 88. Rule No. 86 reads as follows :
By the 54th section of the Imperial Act, 30 Vic., c. 3, 'The British North America Act, 1867.' it is provided that the House shall not adopt or pass any vote, resolution, address or Bill for the appropriation of any part of the public revenue, or of any tax or impost, to any purpose that has not been first recommended by

a message of the Governor General In the session in which such vote, resolution, address or Bill is proposed.
Rule No. 88 is couched iu about the same wording. It requires that no motion can be made in the House for any public aid or charge upon the people unless it be considered in the Committee of the Whole House. I need not refer to the importance of 'the principle embodied in Rule 86. It gives, as we see, the initiation of money votes to the Crown, and was adopted in Canada as a necessary remedy against the numerous and glaring proposals made by private members to make grants of public money, as Mr. Gladstone once said in parliament (vol. 182 ' Hansard,' p. 598).
The principle of Rule 88 is perhaps of not as great importance. In fact, in England to-day they are in the habit of introducing Bills where appropriations of public money are provided for, with the reserve, however, that the clauses which give the public aid or charge upon the people are inserted in italics, and considered as blanks until the House has considered those clauses in committee on a separate resolution. They have a standing order to that effect. Those clauses, however, are so well considered as being part of the Bill, that if they are adopted in committee the Bill is not reported with amendments.
It was decided in England by the ltt. Hon. Mr. Peel, in 1894 :
Provisions imposing charges in a Bill involving charges on the revenue are printed in italics and technically form no part of the Bill, but the discussion thereon Is not irregular. The chairman in committee would nit put any question on those clauses unless the charges to be imposed by them were previously sanctioned in a money committee, and the motion setting up that committee could not be put unless a minister of the Crown signified the Queen's recommendation to such charges being incurred. As the government were not prepared to sign this recommendation, the debate therefore is of the nature of an academical discussion, as no effect can be given to it, but the debate is not irregular.	1 [DOT] - i
In this country we have been following the same procedure. Bourinot says, at page 597 :
It often happens that Bills are introduced with certain clauses providing for salaries or other charges on the public revenue, and in that case the Bill may be introduced directly on motion, while the clauses in question (which should be distinguished by italics or brackets) are considered in the shape of resolutions in committee, and when agreed to, referred to the committee on the Bill.
When the motion for leave was made the other day, I suggested that the debate be adjourned. The House, however, went on to consider the motion for leave, and it was adopted, and the Bill stood over for the second reading on the next day. Since that time a resolution has been put on the Order Paper, having for its object the approval of the contract mentioned in the said Bill,

and, for the purpose of authorizing the government to do whatever is necessary to give full effect to the said Bill. Moreover, the House has been informed of the fact, that the Crown has recommended the said resolution to the House. It has since been adopted and referred to the Committee on the Bill. If at one time the question could have been raised, whether this Bill was properly introduced I do not think that at the present stage of the proceedings it would be a proper question to discuss. We are now aware that the recommendations of the Crown have been given to the money clauses of the Bill, and that they have been considered in Committee. It is perhaps an opportune time to call the attention of the House to a very serious difference which exists between our rules, and those governing the English House of Commons with respect to grants of public money Bills.
Before 1866, the rules 396, 397 and 398 of the parliament of Great Britain and Ireland provided :	That the House could not proceed upon any motion for granting money, or, for any public aid or charge upon the people, unless upon the recommendation of the Crown, and in Committee of the Whole.
It was found, however, that those rules had not the effect desired, and that members were in the habit of having Bills passed contemplating demands upon the public purse, and containing a clause which provided that the necessary expenses should he defrayed out of money hereafter to he voted by parliament. In 1866 it was decided to amend those rules, and to declare that the restriction would apply not only to actual aids and grants, but also to grants and charges payable out of moneys to he provided by parliament.
The debate on that question is very interesting, and will be found in vol. 182, pp. 591, ail'd following. These English rules are now to he found in Standing Orders 57, 58 and 62, as printed in 1901.
In the Bill under consideration, it is provided in clause 22, that no money will he paid until a sufficient appropriation has been made by parliament for the purpose.
Applying to this case the English precedent," as it was before the amendment of 1866, I have come to the conclusion that there was in that respect no violation of our rules 86 and 88.
As to the western section of the road,, the government pledges public credit by guaranteeing the bonds of the company. Could that part of the Bill have been introduced without a previous recommendation of the Crown, and without the consideration of the matters in Committee ?
I find in Blackmore (p. 26), a decision on that point which is to this effect :
A Bill which pledges the public credit for any loan to be raised may be introduced without the preliminary committee, for the introduction of money Bills under the standing orders provided.

that the clauses referring to the raising of the money area guarded by being passed through preliminary committee of the whole House.
Tlie Committee, having adopted a resolution, as required by that decision, and the recommendation of the Crown having been announced, I am of opinion, that the House may proceed to debate, and to adjust the motion for the third reading of the Bill.
We have a precedent in this House in the procedure adopted with regard to the contract with Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann. On the 8th of February, 1898, that contract was laid before the House. At the same time a motion for leave to introduce the Bill confirming the said contract was granted, and before the second reading of the Bill, the House passed a resolution, on the recommendation of His Excellency, providing for the construction of the railway mentioned in the contract. The resolution was reported and referred to the Committee of the Whole, on the Bill.

Bill (No. 237) to further amend the Steamboat Inspection Act, 1898, read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon.
On section 1,
What change in the law is effected by this ?

The explanation of this Bill is very simple. A Bill passed the House and the Senate this session amending the Steamboat Inspection Act. By an inad-vertanee an omission was made from it. A petition had been presented on behalf of people owning or running boats on the Yukon river, and some other rivers in the west, asking permission to use coal oil as fuel. I was under the impression that it could be allowed ; but after looking through the law and studying the precedents, I came to the conclusion that such permission could not be granted legally. Coal oil as fuel has come into very general use, and the officers of my department report that when it is properly stored and guarded it is perfectly safe.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman be kind enough to say what subsection 1 of section 27 really does enact ?

The portion of subsection 1 of section 27, to which this refers, reads as follows :
No coal oil lamp shall be used between decks on any passenger steamboat in which any inflammable material is carried; nor shall any coal oil which will not bear a test of 300 degrees Fahrenheit without taking Are be used on any passenger steamboat.
It is proposed to add at the end of this section ;
Provided, however, that in any case where oil is used as fuel for the production of motive power on steamboats, oil which will bear a test of two hundred degrees Fahrenheit without taking fire may be accepted if properly stored with safe and suitable provisions as to safety and to guard against fire and explosion from such oil to the satisfaction of the steamboat inspector.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: You are changing the test from 300 degrees to 200 degrees ?
Only when it is: used as fuel for motive power.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES :

speechtext: Does uot the danger which was previously guarded against still exist ?

Section 27, as regards the oil to be used for lighting purposes, is left the same. This deals with cases where the oil is used as fuel for the production of motive power. It provides that oil which will bear a test of 200 degrees Fahrenheit may be accepted if properly stored to the satisfaction of the steamboat inspector. Besides, I know as a fact that the insurance companies will not permit the use of the oil for motive power except under special rules and regulations.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Unless the conditions to which the hon. gentleman refers are statutory, we cannot rely on their being enforced or made effective. I understand that the hon. gentleman depends to a great extent on the conditions imposed by insurance companies, but I would not consider that a good principle in legislation. Some of these steamers may not be insured, and if you were to have an accident and loss of life resulting from the absence of safeguards, that would be a very unfortunate condition of affairs.

I have referred to the insurance companies' conditions only as an additional safeguard. Myjion. friend will see that there is provision at the end of this Bill for the taking of proper precautions. The oil must be properly stored, with safe and suitable provisions as to safety and to guard against fire and explosion, to the satisfaction of the steamboat inspector. The test is the same as in the United States, and it is considered perfectly safe, under certain conditions, to use that oil for fuel for motive purpose. The boats on the transportation companies between San Fran-

cisco and Dawson are using that oil at present, under the laws and regulations of the United States, and considered perfectly safe. The officers of my department report that under the conditions imposed by this Bill, there will be no danger.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that in the interests of the navigation of the River St. Lawrence, between Montreal and Quebec, and the River Saguenay below Quebec, to amend the Pilotage Act, and the Acts relating to the Montreal Harbour Commissioners, and the Quebec Harbour Commissioners, so as to place the pilotage of these districts under the control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. R. Prefontaine).

speechtext: Why apply to one part of the country only ?

We have not been able to get the shipping interests in Quebec proper to consent to it. And the harbour commissioners of Quebec and the corporations of pilots themselves do not want it at present. After many consultations with them, I came to the conclusion that we would try the plan of bringing under the control of the department the pilots of the port of Montreal as well as those of the Saguenay river. We will see if it works any better. If it is found to be an improvement, probably these gentlemen in Quebec will consent to an extension of the system. The' Bill covers the upper Saguenay. The reasons are these : There have been serious accidents in the Saguenay river, due to the incompetence and ignorance of some of the pilots. The pilots could not agree with the harbour commissioners of Quebec as regards the pilotage of the Saguenay. The harbour commissioners allowed all pilots to pilot vessels in the Saguenay river, instead of appointing only those who were well acquainted with the river. This resolution is introduced on the recommendation of the shipping interests and the boards of trade of Montreal, who think it would be in the public interest to have the Saguenay river put under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which, while keeping control of the pilots in the district of Quebec, will require from them such examination as will afford the necessary guarantee of efficiency to the shipping interests.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What body has control at Quebec and Montreal, and between the two cities, at the present time ?
The harbour commissioners of Montreal control the pilotage between that city and Quebec, and the harbour commissioners of Quebec control the pilotage of that city and down the gulf to Bic.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Does this Bill remove the pilots between Quebec and Montreal from the jurisdiction of the Montreal harbour commissioners ?
It is proposed to remove the pilotage authority from the harbour commissioners of Montreal to the Department of Marine and Fisheries as concerns the river between Montreal and Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Does that comprise the pilots at Montreal as well ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The resolution does not make that very clear. What you mean hy the resolution is this, that the pilots above Quebec and up to Montreal are placed under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: And the pilots at Quebec and below as far as Bic are to remain under the control of the Quebec harbour commissioners V
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Will there not be something of an anomaly in the government exercising control over the pilots on part of the river and not over these on another part of the river V

The principle is the same. At the present time pilots from Montreal to Quebec are under the control of the Montreal harbour commissioners, and the pilots from Quebec to the gulf are under the control of the Quebec harbour commissioners. It is now proposed to change that system, and to take the control over those in the Montreal district from the Montreal harbour commissioners and vest it in the Department of Marine and Fisheries. This is done with the unanimous consent of the pilots themselves, who are not incorporated between Montreal and Quebec. But between Quebec and the gulf they are incorporated, and that is why they persist in making their own regulations. From Montreal to Quebec they are not incorporated, and are administered by the harbour commissioners of Montreal, and it is desirable to make some further regulations governing those pilots. The harbour commissioners of Montreal are quite willing that this control should pass to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the pilots themselves are unanimously willing, and the boards of trade and the shipping interests have been asking for this amendment for years. The Act will go into effect on the 1st of January next, after regulations have been prepared and submitted to the different bodies interested, so that the interests of every one will be fully protected.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What is the reason that the pilots between Montreal and Quebec are not Incorporated ? What is the difference between those below Quebec and those above ?*

Those between Montreal and Quebec asked two years ago to be incorporat-Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
ed, and presented a Bill for that purpose. It was opposed by the boards of trade and those interested in navigation, and the Bill was killed in the Senate. That is the reason why they are not a corporation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: But if there is any need of putting the control of the pilots under the Department of Marine and Fisheries for one portion of the river, the same argument will apply to all.

The hon. gentleman may be right in theory, but we do not want to put any compulsion upon the pilots at and below Quebec, who are now making a strong opposition to coming under the control of the department, and the shipping interest in Quebec are supporting them. So we have concluded to take only those of the Montreal district under our own control, and to make such regulations as will be satisfactory to the public and to the pilots themselves. If these work satisfactorily, as we expect they will, we will then be justified in saying to the pilots of the Quebec district, whether you are-willing or not, you must come under the control of another authority. But for the present we are not ready to do that.

speechtext:
The difference between the pilots on the river between Quebec and' Montreal and those from Quebec down to Bic Station is easily explained. It was only a couple of years ago that the pilots of Montreal moved for incorporation ; their system is entirely different from that of the other pilots and is almost voluntary, giving the shipping companies the privilege of choosing whom they liked out of the
number of pilots. There are about seventy-five pilots between Montreal and Quebec and the best authorities say that about twenty-five or thirty could do the work. As to the pilots between Quebec and Bic, I may say that they form a body which has existed over one hundred years, and as a corporation for forty-three years. I think it is generally agreed that we should move slowly in this matter, that we should experiment first and find out if the new plan works well between Quebec and Montreal before we go any further with it. I want to read you a few extracts which I hold in my hand as to the history of the pilots of Quebec :
The branch pilots for the lower St. Lawrence, the sea pilots, were incorporated in 1860. At that time, the pilotage authority was the Trinity House. Later in 1875 this was replaced by the harbour commission. (Vide chapter 82.) Our corporation has been in existence for over 43 years, so that it has had a long experience in pilotage matters as well as in all that concerns the management of the pilots under its control and direction. It is perfectly well posted as to the services of the different pilotage stations such as~Bic and Father Point, as well as what is necessary in handling the ocean steamships, and the vessels called colliers. Besides this, our corporation has a considerable advantage, by its constant communications with the captains of the pilot-boats who are themselves branch pilots always cruising day and night to Bio and other stations. In brief, its duty is to see that the service is as effective as possible. This year the number of pilots on official list is 114, but the effective number is, in reality, 106.
I may say, Mr. Chairman, that at the time of incorporation the number of pilots was between 240 and 250, and in order to explain this diminution, I may say that it is now admitted that probably seventy-five or eighty pilots could do all the work between Quebec and Bic, owing to the change which has taken place in the system of navigation, owing to the introduction of steamships. At one time all of the vessels were sailing ships which moved very slowly, but with the more rapidly moving steamships the same pilot can do five times as much work as he then could.
The pilot office is open the year rcund. During the season of navigation, that is to say, from April 10th to December lOih, our office Is open day and night. The night watchman is himself a licensed pilot, always ready to give all the information asked for at any time. He has always on hand some pilots ready to board a vessel the moment she arrives in port, be It a sailing ship or a steamer, whether she comes from Montreal, or Three Rivers, or whether she is ready to leave our port for sea.
The ship-owners, their agents, the captains or masters have the right of selecting their pilots in the port of Quebec or at the pilotage stations at Bic or Father Point. Every spring I the large companies choose the pilots they wish I to have and our board readily accede to their request, reserving the right, however, to com-i mand their withdrawal if the general interest

taught to them otherwise. This would cost very little to the government and would make the'navigation of our river safer. These apprentices could then make the necessary soundings, under the direction of a licensed pilot._ The pliot hoard should be authorized to examine at least once a year, during the summer all the apprentices. This would give us the opportunity of seeing the progress made by them in the study of their future profession. Special notes would be kept in a particular book to that effect? I cannot repeat too often that the profession is open to every one. It is, therefore, unfair to say, as is said in some quarters, that the profession is limited to certain persons only. We have actually on our board, a pilot who has been several years president of our-corporation, and whose father was never a pilot. Some say: it is only the pilot's sons who can enter the profession. Does it not happen often that a young man becomes a lawyer, or a doctor because his father belonged to the profession. He undergoes the influence where he lives. It is the same thing with the pilot's sons ; from their tender youth they hear navigation talked of ; they Live small boats, which they command with their comrades and, little by little, the taste developes for navigation, and they become pilots. Where is the evil in that ?
According to the new law the apprentices are admitted to be indentured with the corporation of pilots only after permission is obtained from the pilotage authority as to the number. These apprentices are presented to the pilot board, according to their seniority, by licensed pilots, after the manner which has now been made law. They are afterwards presented by the board of directors to the pilotage authority who has a right to accept or refuse them. These apprentices are then seemingly under the government control, because all the by-laws, even those of the pilots before coming into force, have to be published in both languages in the newspapers, and receive the sanction of the pilotage authority established by the government.
The tariff.-The pilotage tariff go is as far back as 1803. It has 100 years of existence. It is only in 1882 that we succeeded in getting its lightly modified. We were then granted an increase of 7J per cent ; the harbour comm's-sion have unanimously and according to law, recommended 5 per cent. Besides we had from the Hon. Mr. McLelan, the then Minister of Marine, the promise that in the following year our tariff would be based on the tonnage, in all the Dominion. This manner is undoubtedly the most rational. Several of the ministers who have preceded you at the head of the ministry, have admitted the principle, but that is all that has been done ; it has been a dead letter.
You will admit that the conditions of life have singularly changed. Every thing costs dearer, and we are still with an old tariff 100 years old, slightly changed in 1882. But the lawyer's anl the notary's, and the salaries of the judges, have been changed on the ground that the cost _ of life has much increased. We are mortals like all these men, and we suffer from the increase in the cost of living as they do. Would it not be just to remodel our tariff ?
It is a fundamental principle that an employee has a right to such remuneration, in proportion to the responsibility he assumes. Does a lawyer entrusted with a $100,000 case charge the same fee as for a 100 case ? Evidently not. Well,
why not apply this rule to us. If it is just for some, it ought to be just for others.
Allow me to call your attention to the fact that we have lost, partially at least, what was granted to us in 1882, by the exemption of colliers from pilotage (vide R.S.C., chapter 80, section 59, (C) and by 2 Ed. VII., chapter 27). Some of these colliers take pilots, but some take pilots only when the captains fear that they could not easily pilot the vessels themselves or believe that they would save time by taking a licensed pilot. We have already verified the incompetency of these unqualified mariners, especially when crossing another ship in the river in different places. Our pilots know what to do being constantly exposed to these crossings, they-know how to give the necessary spice, because they are certain of the depth of the water they have on either side of the river. There is loss of time for both parties and those inexperienced pilots put our pilots in difficult positions.
The pilot, to have a right to take charge of any vessel, must be a branch pilot. That is to say, he must have served an apprenticesh p of seven consecutive years, made eight trips over the Atlantic, have passed an examination as to the river, and as to his sight, hearing, &c. When an accident happens to him, his branch is taken from him for a longer or shorter period, if not for life. As to those colliers, said to be exempted from pilotage, any one can take charge of them without having passed an examination, or having proved that he had a sufficient knowledge of the river, and yet he has no responsibility, as there ie no law governing such a case. We keep license! pilots at the pilotage stations on the pilot ^boats ready to take charge of these vehsels. We believe it would be better to repeal that law. After all, the pilots have never refused service, so conscious are they of the responsibility of their position.
The whole is respectfully submitted.
(Sgd.) L. E. MORIN,
President of the corporation of pilots for and below the harbour of Quebec.
I may add that some 35 or 40 years ago, when we had only wooden sailing vessels, the pilots were paid so much per foot draught. In those days the largest sailing vessels carried a cargo of from 1,200 to 1,500 tons. To-day vessels on the St. Lawrence carry from 8,000 to 10,000 tons. Then, wooden vessels sailing down the St. Lawrence might go aground five or six times without any injury, while the vessels of to-day, being constructed of iron or steel, will be smashed by the least shock. Then, the wooden vessels usually had only the wind for their propelling power, while the vessels of today are steamers. Therefore, the responsibility of the pilots is to-day much greater than it was formerly.
This paper, in a few words, describes the action of the pilots on the Lower St. Lawrence. No one who has bad any knowledge of the navigation of that river from Quebec down will deny that the corporation of pilots is composed of excellent men. They are all men of experience who have bad a thorough training as sailors, who know all about the compass and the business of navigation, and who have been over the seas In many parts of the world. There is no doubt

that in the last few years great improvements have been made on the St. Lawrence river, but some things yet remain to be dione. It is admitted that there are more pilots now belonging to the corporation of pilots from Quebec down than are able to And employment. As the steamship companies have their choice of pilots, it would be a very good thing if the Department of Marine and Fisheries employed the balance to take constant soundings across and up and down the channel. They would be able to make complete reports from year to year, which would certainly be valuable aids in the navigation of the St. Lawrence, aud would tend to diminish the chances of accidents.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I fail to see what the argument of my hon. friend from Bellecliasse (Mr. Talbot) has to do with the resolution now before the House. I agree fully with what he says with respect to the great body of the pilots; and some legislation may be necessary at the proper time on their behalf. But the resolution now before the House is to amend the Pilotage Act and the Acts relating to the Montreal Harbour Commissioners and the Quebec Harbour Commissioners. I fully agree with my hon. friend from St. Anne's division, Montreal (Mr. Gallery). The government should move slowly in disturbing existing arrangements on the St. Lawrence. It is very singular that after the House has been in session for nearly seven months, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries should have the Order paper covered with four resolutions which he is introducing at this late date, and on which Bills will afterwards be founded. What time is there for the harbour commissioners of Montreal andi Quebec and the general shipping interests to protest against this resolution if they do not approve of it.
They have all demanded it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
We have not seen any evidence of that demand, and we have the hon. member for St. Anns (Mr. Gallery), who represents one of the districts most largely Interested, protesting against it. But there is a sting in the closing words of the resolution, ' so as to place the pilotage of these districts under the control of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries.' Are we to take this as carrying out in part the pledge which the hon. minister made to his constituents before his election, when he said to them : If you will elect me, I am going to take control of a great portion of the public Works Department? If he made that speech With the sanction of the government, why does not the government come down with a Bill to divide up the Department of Public Works, instead of bringing in resolutions by piece-meal to transfer portions of that department from the Minister of Public Works to the hon. gentleman ? We have here a resolution to take this pilotage system and Mr. TALBOT.
put it under the control of the Marine Department. The hon. minister violated a cabinet secret in making the announcement he did, and afterwards denied that he had made any such declaration, but we find the announcement verified by this resolution. I should think that the words of the hon. member for St. Anns would have some weight with the government, and that the government would hesitate before disturbing the existing regulations. The present system has been in force for years, and I fail to see what necessity there is for changing it. f this is in part accomplishment of the bargain made by the government with the hon. minister before he accepted office, namely, that they would transfer a certain portion of the public works to his department, they should come down with a Bill and do it in the light of day, and not slip in half a dozen little resolutions taking this part and the other away by piece-meal from tire Public Works Department and transferring them to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. I would advise the government to let this Bill lay over until we hear from the pilots, and the shipping interests, and the harbour commissioners. They are under the Public Works Department now, do they want to come under the control of the Marine Department ? These interests connected with navigation should either be in one department or the other, and not be split up piecemeal-a part in Public Works, a part in Marine and Fisheries and a part in Railways and Canals. The government should settle on some well defined plan and place them under the charge of one department, so that the people would know with whom they were dealing.

The tea son I raised an objection was because I think the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal are just ns well able to manage their own affairs as are the Harbour Commissioners of the port of Quebec. I fail to see why the pilotage system and the pilots below Quebec should be treated differently from the pilotage system and pilots between Montreal and Quebec. I have been speaking to a couple of Harbour Commissioners since the House took recess at six o'clock, and I find that they are of the same opinion as myself, and would like to have the matter held over for a day or two.
I am not at all implying that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine has any object to serve in doing this. I believe that he is simply acting according to the wish of the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal, but I am not inclined to see the matter in the same light as these gentlemen. In my opinion we would be taking a retrograde course, if we were to take this matter out of their hands and give it to the control of the Marine Department. It would be better that the resolution should be held over a day or two in any case, so as to give us time to think over it.

I do not quite approve of the way in which my hon. friend the Minister of Marine approaches this question. He says that because a certain public body has no objection to transferring to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the contrql of the pilotage from Montreal to Quebec, this should be done, and because a certain other public body does not want the pilotage from Quebec down to be interferred with, no change should be made. It seems to me that the real question is what is the most effective way of dealing with the pilotage question. If the most effective way is to put it under the control of the hon. gentleman's department, then let that be done for the entire pilotage from Montreal down to Bic. If it is best to let matters remain under the present control, then make .no change. I do not see why this matter should be dealt with upon any consideration other than the consideration of what is best in the public interest. But the only reason which my hon. friend gives for the change is that certain men, who are exercising certain functions in Montreal, are willing that the pilots under their' jurisdiction should fall under the control of his department. Is there any sound principle in that for the administration of public affairs ?
The principle involved is the same in the two cases. I entirely agree with my hon. friend that the whole of the pilotage should be under the control of the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I did not say that it should be under the control of the department, but that we should come to a conclusion as to what would be the best plan, and when we came to a conclusion apply that to the whole river.
Who is going to judge ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Why the government.
On the advice of whom ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: On whose advice does the government act with regard to public affairs generally ?
Public opinion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Is there one public opinion for the river above Quebec and another below ?
The -MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. Yes.

That is not my conception of public opinion. If my hon. friend means that there are local opinions in each case, each of which differs from the other, I can understand him. But that is not public opinion. Further in matters of administration. I do not agree with
the hon. minister or my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) that you are to be guided entirely by public opinion. The government ought to have some opinion of its own. Surely my hon. friend does not propose that, if public opinion this year is favourable to dealing with this question in a certain way, he will deal with it in that way this year, and, if public opinion in that particular district veers around, he will veer with it and deal with the matter in another way next year. I know that public opinion controls the policy of the government in very many cases; it controls it much more than principles do. But I do think, so far as an administrative matter of this kind is concerned, no safe guide is to be found in the mere question of local public opinion in one locality.

But, when we find among those interested a unanimous opinion in favour of a change in the way suggested by this resolution, I think the government is perfectly justified in accepting the suggestion of those who know something about the matter. For instance, the shipping conference of Montreal is composed of men representing the different steamship companies. That conference have represented time and again that the pilotage system between Montreal and Quebec should be under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and that there should be an improvement in the management of this important part of the St. Lawrence transportation system. That has been their opinion, to my knowledge for the last ten or fifteen years. An investigation took place some years ago, the 1'esult of which was that the recommendation that the pilotage should be put under the control of the government. It was not done because the government wanted to have the consent, as much as possible, of those who are directly interested. There were the board of harbour commissioners of Montreal and the pilots. The pilots are an important body of men. Most of them have made sacrifices in studying navigation and becoming proficient for the woTk they are called upon to do. After becoming Minister of Marine and Fisheries I took hold of this question, because I knew something of it before I was in office, having been a member of the board of harbour commissioners of Montreal for four years. I knew the difficulties in connection with this part of the navigation of the St. Lawrence. The board of harbour commissioners came to the conclusion that they would be relieved of part of their duties by handing over the control of pilotage to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, and they unanimously passed a resolution in that sense. The pilots themselves discussed the question for quite a long time before coming to a decision, and. finally, they came unanimously to the decision that they should be under the control of the department. The

Board of Trade of Montreal also favours the change. These are all public bodies and must know something of what is in the public interest and in the interest of the navigation of the St. Lawrence, that part of it at least. But we have not succeeded in convincing the Harbour Commissioners of Quebec or those specially interested in navigation in Quebec that they should concur in this Bill. They have a corporation of pilots, and that corporation hold to their privileges and advantages, believing that the severe laws and regulations under which they work are sufficient. They have not consented to come under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. Why should we coerce them ? Why should we take them by the throat and force them to come under the control of the department when, after all it is a debatable question and a question which, even when it is decided in the sense in which the government have decided it up to this point, will involve some difficulty in working out so as to make sure that it shall be to the general advantage ? The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal are convinced, the pilots themselves are convinced, the board of trade and all the shipping interests are convinced that the pilots should be under the control of the department, because then they would know whom to blame in case of an accident or in case incompetent pilots are employed. Under these circumstances, the government have prepared this Bill. Delay is suggested. I do not know how anybody can complain about haste when everybody agrees to this measure and demands it. It is very well for the hon. member for Ste. Anne, Montreal (Mr. Gallery) to voice the after thought of some members of the harbour commissioners in asking for a day or two more. But surely this hon. gentleman is not serious any more than the hon. member for Leeds (Mi-. Taylor) is serious in his remarks. Because, when everybody wants something to be done, and all have agreed that it should be done, I would like to know if the objection is well founded when it comes from outside. Who knows better what is proper for the pilotage between Montreal and Quebec than the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal ? Who knows better than the pilots ? Who knows better than the representatives of the shipping interest ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: If they are left to themselves. But the hon. minister stated that he had not been able to convince the harbour interests of Quebec that it would be in the interests of navigation. So, it is evident that the department has been trying to influence public opinion. The framing of public opinion originated with the Department of Marine and Fisheries by the hon. minister's own story.

That would indicate powerful influence on the part of the department. I Hon. Mr. PREFONTAINE.
stated a fact that was well known, and with regard to which I defy contradiction, when I said that for over ten years the shipping interests of Montreal had been asking for what I propose in this Bill. Who are more interested in the safe navigation between Quebec and Montreal than the shipping interest ? They are unanimous on the subject. Why should the hon. gentleman say that we had framed public opinion in that sense ? We have not framed it. Their opinion of the shipping interest on this question was formed ten years ago and it has never changed. But the pilots themselves were not at first disposed to favour the change. Lately they have convinced themselves that it would be better in their own interests that they should be under the control of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. The board of trade have passed a resolution in that sense and so has the harbour commissioners. So, opinion among those interested is unanimous. Outsiders certainly cannot be supposed to know more than those who are especially interested in a satisfactory settlement of this question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Prefoutaine) has hot assigned a very high function to my hon. friend from Ste. Anne's division (Mr. Gallery) when he says that everyone is asking for this Bill and demanding it.
Every one interested.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is not my hon. friend from Ste. Anne's division a ratepayer of Montreal ?
He is not interested in shipping.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is not the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gallery) representative of one of the most important divisions of Montreal ? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries practically tells us that the hon. gentleman is not to be considered, because though he stands up and objects to this proposal, the hon. minister says that everybody demands it.
Every one interested.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I should have thought that my hon. friend from St. Anne's division, being representative of a very important division of the city of Montreal, might be regarded as being interested, to some slight extent at least. I do not know how many constituents my hon. friend has,' I suppose, 35,000 "or 40,000, for whom he speaks in this House, and yet he is not interested in this measure, which affects the interest of the city of Montreal to a vital extent. Well, no one is talking about forcing the pilots, or doing them anv injustice, either at Montreal or Quebec. The' pilots at Montreal and Quebec must be

subject to the law. The passing of an Act regulating the control of these pilots would not necessarily result in any injustice to them. Is it to be supposed that the pilots coming under the control of a department of this government would thereby be subjected to some injustice ? Would it disturb their corporate rights in any way ? Would they, by being subjected to an Act of that kind, be treated any more harshly than any railway or telephone company, any bank, any company having public officers in its employ, is treated by being made subject to the law, and to regulations devised by the government under the law ? This is not to be spoken of as coercion, this is to be spoken of as a regulation in the public interest, such a regulation as will protect the public interest on the one hand, and will also do justice to the officers engaged in the performance of public duties on the other hand.

I think the point under discussion as to the different position occupied by the Quebec pilots and the Montreal pilots, should be made clear. The hon. member for Bast Grey (Mr. Sproule) doubted whether the memorandum I read from the pilots' corporation of Quebec was germane to the question. I began my remarks by saying that they were unanimously of the opinion in Quebec, the pilots the harbour commissioners and the shipping interests, that things should remain as they are now, whilst in Montreal they are just as unanimously asking for a change. The pilots of Quebec are differently organized altogether from those at Montreal. In the latter district they have a system of go-as-you-please, each one is independent of the others: whilst in Quebec they are under stringent rules, being bound by their Act of incorporation. Besides that, the Quebec pilots are making strong efforts every year to improve the St. Lawrence river in order to make the navigation more efficient. The change they ask for is contained in that memorandum. All the pilots are interested in preventing accidents as far as possible, because their lives are at stake in the performance of their duties, and the welfare cf their wives and children is at stake. When a man takes a steamer and is on duty 12 or 15 hours, he may run into a fog and meet with an accident. Well, you may say, he hadi no business to run into a fog. But he must suffer the consequences, and in any case he is set aside by the steamship company, whether he was blameable or not. 'mat man is certainly interested in seeing that everything possible is done for the improvement of navigation, he is interested in seeing that every facility is given to the safe navigation of vessels.
Do steamship companies have the selection of their pilots in going out and coming in ?
Yes.
Are they not obliged to take the first pilot that hails them on coming in ?

No. Each steamship company in Quebec has an agent or a representative, who goes to the pilot corporation and says : We require so many pilots this year, and we want you to give us the names of those whom you think are the best pilots, and we will take our choice. The company keeps these pilots on trial a number of months, perhaps a year. Indeed some of these pilots have been forty years with the same company, who are satisfied with their services and who employ them all the time. When an agent gets a telegram notifying him that a steamer is coming in, he asks the pilot to go down to Father Point and take charge of the vessel. The agent has the choice of the pilot.

I should think that is a very serious state of affairs, because, according to my hon. friend's statement, it appears that the steamship companies have the choice of their own pilots, and if these pilots are not willing to violate the law by running into a fog, or runniug at an excessive speed, they are put to one side and others are put in their places. That indicates that some be.tter regulations are needed in the district of Quebec.

It is not the fault of the pilots, because if the pilots were left to themselves they would prefer throwing out the anchor than to move on under dangerous circumstances. But they have got to move in their own interest.

I agree that, under these conditions, it is not the fault of the pilots, but it is the fault of the system, and indicates that some different regulations are required. I do not say that the system which prevails in Halifax is a perfect one, but it is a different one. I have a little familiarity with the system prevailing there. Vessels coming into the harbour of Halifax are obliged to take the first pilot that hails them. But the pilots are under strict regulations. No pilot receives ai license unless he is perfectly competent, and they are employed only so long as proper discipline is maintained among them, and every case of wrong-doing is properly punished. We have a pilot commission inj Halifax that attends to these matters. Then when a vessel leaves the city the same pilot that brought the vessel in is to be on hand to 'Sake her out, and if he is on hand the vessel is obliged to engage the service of that same pilot for the voyage out.
Under the system in Halifax, the pilot who does no work, is he not entitled to as much compensation as the pilot who does work ?

The pilots are obliged to be on duty; they are obliged to be on hand when vessels are likely to come into port. A vessel is bound to take the pilot that first offers, as I understand the regulations, and that pilot has the option of taking that vessel to sea himself. He is bound to be on hand when she goes out, and if he is not, he is subject to censure and punishment. I think there is some system by which the pilots, although they do not happen to meet a vessel in the first instance, nevertheless receive some consideration for the time they have spent, and for the risk which they have run in going out to the mouth of the harbour in all kinds of weather to pick up vessels that are coming in. I think they also have a provision by which some portion of the common fund is set aside as a superannuation allowance for those pilots who are no longer able to perform their duty. But I think the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) will agree that it is not in the interest of the pilots themselves that any such system as that which he describes should prevail, and it seems to me one of the strongest arguments why some better regulations should be made respecting pilotage affairs in the district of Quebec. Whatever else we may differ about we are all agreed that there should be no such system as will place temptation in the way of pilots to violate the rules which are laid down for the proper guidance of vessels. If a captain of a vessel desires to run the risk of violating the regulations in order to get to sea a little earlier, I say that the pilot should be in a perfectly independent position, and be at liberty to disobey the captain and to say that he will not violate the regulations; he should be able to do that without the slightest fear of penalty. I think the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will agree with that. If the system to-day be as described by my hon. friend from Bellechasse, it is certainly the best argument in favour of better regulations.

In answer to the hon. the leader of the opposition I may say that after a pilot starts with a vessel he may anchor the vessel if he wishes whether the captain is willing or not. While the pilot is in charge of the vessel he is the master, but there is this consideration that the captain looks after his own interests ; he has so much expense for delays, Ac. for which he has to account. The company want him to make time and he is urged to make time and to save expenses so that the pilot is indirectly under that influence. The one body that should see that a vessel comes to anchor in cases of that kind is the insurance compafly. It is they who suffer the risk and the' loss and they should see to this matter. They know all about the situation and know that this occurs for the very reason that the pilots at Quebec always take their steamers at night. The naviga-
Mr. EMMERSON,
ti m between Montreal and Quebec is carried on during the day time and the steamer arrives at Quebec about dark so that the Quebec pilot has to do his work in the night.

My hon. friend will see that it is the public who suffer in the end, because as the result of this, accidents occur, insurance rates are put up and the St. Lawrence route is discredited.
Resolution reported, read the first and second time, and agreed to.
Moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 261). *especting the Pilotage District of Montreal and respecting the Pilotage District of Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. (Hon. Raymond Prefontaine).

speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution ;
Resolved, that It is expedient, in the interests of the harbour of North Sydney, Nova Scotia, to amend chapter 30 of the statutes of 1879, intituled : ' An Act respecting the Harbour of North Sydney In Nova Scotia,' by strik-ink out the word ' four ' in the last line of section 8 of the said Act, and substituting therefor the word ' five ' ; and by inserting the words ' after deducting five per cent for his remuneration ' after the word ' shall ' in the fourth line of section 10 of the said Act.
Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to explain.

I am perfectly willing to give all the information but I really cannot give more than is contained in the resolution. It appears that the harbour commission of North Sydney, Nova Scotia, have more work to do than they used to have and their secretary will not remain in office with a salary of $400. The department lias been requested to amend the law so as to give a salary of $500. The second section provides that the collector of customs, who has been collecting harbour dues, will have a commission of five per cent of these dues as remuneration for his services.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is there any remuneration provided for the commissioners themselves either at Sydney or North Sydney ?
I do not think they have any remuneration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Is my hon. friend quite sure of that ?

The commissioners have no>
remuneration whatever. With that commission of five per cent the collector of customs will probably receive $150 a year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND IISHERIES.

speechtext: Has my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries considered the question of giving some moderate remuneration to pilotage authorities in cases where the duties which they discharge make very large demands upon their time ? I know the question has come up a good many times within the last ten or twelve years in connection with the pilotage authority at Halifax and I believe it was under the consideration of one of the predecessors of my hon. friend, Sir Louis Davies. I do not know whether my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries has himself taken the question into consideration.

No requests have been made of me in regard to that, but, I will inquire into it.
