Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer a few remarks to the House With reference to a matter which is one, in my estimation, of considerable importance, the consideration of which has been delayed until this stage of the session. Naturally the House will not be disposed to devote much time to it at present, and I shall certainly not trespass to any extent on its forbearance. We discussed last session the propi-iety of making a grant for a polar expedition, and I think that the general feeling of the House was in favour of a sufficient grant being made for that purpose. At an early date in the session, a very large 401}
and influential deputation waited upon the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, accompanied by Captain Bernier, whose explanation of the plan he intended to adopt was evidently quite satisfactory to the minister, and it was expected that some action would be taken on his application. I do not know what the intention of the government may be, but it certainly has not moved in that direction up to the present. The importance of this expedition, I think, is very great indeed. A successful expedition to the pole would give to Canada a very prominent place among the maritime states, and the discovery of the Pole would give us a standing with regard to territorial acquisition in the north between the Pole and the north-rn coast of the continent, which we would not otherwise have. A successful expedition would be worth much more than it would cost, and an unsuccessful one would entail no disgrace, because the discovery of the North Pole has been the dream of nations for many years, and each failure to reach the goal has only been an incitement to a renewed attempt. Captain Bernier reminds me, in his persistence of Columbus going from court to court in Europe in the 15th century, seeking for a patron to put him in possession of the means of making his coveted voyage of discovery to the west. For several years Captain Bernier has been in pursuit of this project. His persistence is worthy of all praise, and the traits of character he has evinced in the prosecution of his mission would lead us to suppose that he has the dogged pertinacity and courage which would staud him in good stead, if he ever be placed in command of a Canadian Polar expedition. He has peculiarly good qualifications for this position. He is now fifty-one years of age. He commanded a vessel at the age of seventeen, and has been a commander of 40 vessels. He has crossed the ocean 174 times, and he is a navigator possessing a record. This question of Arctic exploration has engaged his attention the last twenty-four years. He has been a diligent student of all the facts that have been elicited with regard to Arctic matters. He has studied the question of the Arctic currents and the proper methods to be followed in order to make progress towards the North Pole, and his speculation and knowledge have been availed of by Arc-tie explorers, among them Nansen and Baldwin. The route which Captain Bernier proposes to take is to enter the Arctic ocean from the Behring straits. The Japan current strikes the west coast of America, and one portion is deflected to the south and another passes through the Behring straits to the Arctic sea. It has been discovered) that the ice pack in the Arctic ocean moves to the eastward from the western side of the ocean reached from the Pacific ocean, through Behring straits. In 1879 the ' Jeannette ' entered the Arctic ocean at Behring straits, and entered the ice pack,

and while the expedition was disastrous, a portion of the crew reaching the coast of Siberia, the relics of the vessel were afterwards found between Greenland and Spitz-enburg, showing that the ice carried it across the Arctic sea. Captain Bernier proposes to place his vessel in the ice pack, between longitude 170 and 175, entering the Arctic ocean through Behring straits, and trusting to nature for the driving of his vessel as near as possible to the Pole. The old theory about an	open	sea around the	Poleis an exploded one. It is certain now that	if there	is not land	there,the North	Pole	is	water covered	with
ice.
Captain Bernier belongs to a race eminent as exploiters in the early history of this country-a race of adventurers, a race of men filled	with	the	spirit of adventure.
While the English were quietly settling along the sea-board of the Atlantic in the thirteen colonies, and penetrating no farther than the Alleghany Mountains, the French inhabitants of Canada penetrated the far west, established trading stations on _ the upper lakes and on the Upper Mississippi, extended their explorations far beyond Manitoba even, and entertained dreams of the creation of a French empire in that country of the possibilities of which they alone were aware. The captain is thoroughly imbued with that spirit ; and, if he is entrusted *with the charge of this expedition, I have not the slightest doubt that he will be able to give a good account of himself.
One feature of this matter which possesses some degree of significance is the fact that Lord Strathcona endorses the captain's theory with regard to the proper course to pursue in polar explorations. Lord Strathcona has promised to give the Captain a subscription of $5,000, and, by this course and by his statements made to the Captain, has endorsed the plan that Captain Bernier has adopted. This is significant because of the fact that Lord Strathcona is intimately [DOT] acquainted with Arctic matters. He was early in the service of the Hudson Bay Company, has been in the far north, and has a knowledge of that country of a character which makes him peculiarly a judge of the proper methods to be employed in such an expedition as this.
The prize of the discovery of the North Pole is one that any of the great marine powers would gladly win. Several expeditions are even now afoot, as expeditions have been set afoot from time to time, none of which have been successful. It is not an unworthy object of ambition for us to seek to snatch these laurels from other competitors. The Captain's plan is to have the vessel built and owned by the government. This vessel, if she returns from her voyage of exploration, will he of service to the government. She would be the kind of vessel that would be exactly wanted in patrolling Hudson bay, in making voyages Mr. CHARLTON.
among the islands north of Hudson bay* and taking possession of newly discovered lands in that region. The government could easily find useful and profitable employment for such a vessel. The cost of such a vessel as the Captain proposes would be about $80,000. In addition there would be certain instruments required, which, it is supposed, the government has in its possession and could loan along with the vessel, for the purpose of this expedition. In addition to the cost of the vessel and the instruments, about $70,000 additional would be required for the expedition. This the Captain would furnish himself; that is, he would secure it by contribution from the public. About $00,000 has already been secured, and there would be no difficulty in collecting the balance if the government would make the appropriation necessary for the construction of the vessel and would embark upon the scheme as the Captain proposes.
Of course, this vessel would be one of peculiar construction. In the first place she would be built of wood, for a wooden vessel is infinitely better in contact with ice than steel or iron. She would be a vessel of great strength, braced with heavy timbers, and would have six water tight compartments. She would be a vessel of 300 tons register, 120 feet in length, with 35 feet beam, a depth of 18 feet, and would draw1 14 feet of water. She would have an engine of 200 horse power. She would have a ten foot wheel, and would carry 300 tons of anthracite coal of which she would burn 34 tons in twenty-four hours. In every way the vessel would be thoroughly adapted to the navigation of the ice-bound sea. She would carry a spare wheel and a spare rudder. She would carry a diving apparatus, which, I believe, no previous Arctic expedition has carried. She would have 100 tons of provisions-six years' supply. These provisions would be of a character to provide against that drpadful disease of Arctic exploration-scurvy. The provisions would include vegetables of various kinds done up in fifty pound cans; and generally the provisions would be of such a character as to ensure the crew against the ravages of scurvy. She would be-which is a new feature-lighted and heated by electricity. For this purpose she would be furnished with two windmills and two dynamos which would be run by the windmills. The electricity would be used for lighting and heating and also for medical treatment of certain maladies among the crew as, for instance, rheumatism. The vessel would carry a doctor and apparatus for the medical treatment of disease where it might be necessary. This provision with regard to heating and lighting is a matter of very great importance. Of course, the burning of oil. or the combustion of fuel, consumes air, while electric lighting and heating would consume no air. So that keeping the air pure would be much easier by this method of lighting and

heating than by the burning of oil or coal. The vessel also would be kept cheerful and dry, overcoming a great difficulty of former Arctic expeditions, that of dampness in the vessel. The vessel would carry an apparatus for the distilling of water. In most cases, Arctic explorers have depended upon melted snow, which is often found to give a supply of water that is impure and deleterious to the health of the crew. The vessel would carry a wirelesss telegraph apparatus and could maintain communication with some point upon the shore of America, and, when well advanced on the exploration, with some point in Norway. But the great advantage of the wireless system would be that the communication could be maintained with the sledge parties sent out from the vessel. It is the intention of the Captain, as he drifts towards his destination, to send sledge parties fifty miles from the vessel on each side and take soundings at intervals and make other investigations. These sledge parties would be in communication, by wireless telegraphy with the vessel, so that they would know the location of the vessel and the vessel would; know the location of the sledge par-, ties, and the sledge parties -could keep up communication which would be of the greatest importance in -case of emergency of any kind. When the vessel approaches the pole-it might be one hundred miles or two hundred miles away; Nansen, I believe reached within 280 miles of the pole and the nearest has been 250 miles-when the vessel is at its nearest point to the pole a sledge party would be sent out with the most ample and up-to-date provision for making a successful journey over the ice. Among other things, the Captain proposes to have an automobile motor with either a reservoir of electricity or an engine run by gasoline. They would take frames and canvas for boats that could be set up readily for transportation across the open stretches of water. The expedition would set up bamboo rods with small flags every mile, and every ten miles they would place a hollow cylinder with records. Every ten miles also they would leave a supply of provisions, so that the return could be made with greatest speed and safety. And all the time communication with the vessel would be maintained by telegraph.
The Captain proposes to carry a crew of 15 men. and the arrangement with regard to this crew is one to secure efficiency and economy. I will give, from the statement made last year, as to the composition of this crew :
The crew will consist of fifteen men. There will be the commander himself, without pay. There will be two officers, captains of experience. who can take the wheel, go to the masthead and look-out, or perform any duty regarding the navigation or care of the ship in case of the captain being Incapacitated. There will be a first mate who will he what is termed an ice master, a man who is thoroughly conversant with everything pertaining to the dangers of ice and of being caught between the ice floes. There will be two engineers ; one will be a machinist who can do any work in connection with the machinery or apparatus, the telegraph apparatus or fixtures ; while the other will he an electrician and wireless telegraph operator. Two men will be surveyors and astronomers who will also serve on sledge journeys or in almost any other capacity on the vessel. There will be one doctor who will be a botanist and seaman. There will he one naturalist, who will be a botanist, photographer and artist and assistant to the surveyors and electrician, and who also will go on sledge journeys. There will be one cook, who, in addition to being a cook and steward will be an able seaman. There will be one seaman who will be a whaler and sealer and stoker, and who will combine the qualifications of all three and be able to serve in almost any capacity. There will be a carpenter who will also be an able seaman, and one stoker who will also he an able seaman. These will he his crew of 15, men combining the qualifications and different kinds of capacities that, if confined in each case to one man, would require a crew of 50 or 60 men, an efficient crew, and yet a compact crew of small number.
This is the arrangement that Captain Bernier proposes to make with regard to his crew. His scheme for provisioning liis vessel, fitting it out, and the conduct of his expedition, all has been carefully thought out. He has brought to bear upon the arrangement of his plans the experience of a navigator of over thirty years, and his experience as a navigator with regard to Arctic matters extending over more than twenty years. Undoubtedly Captain Bernier possesses qualifications for the task he desires to undertake at least equal to those possessed by any living nautical man. He does not know but deems it advisable to buy the celebrated vessel the ' Fram,' which is for sale, and can be bought at a less price probably than he could construct a vessel. It might be possible to buy the German vessel, the ' Gosse,' which is just returning from an Antarctic expedition. But whatever course may be taken with regard to a vessel, the government is called upon, if it embarks in this scheme, to supply not more than $80,000. It will be an investment in a vessel which will belong to itself, and which will be available in subsequent years for other purposes. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the feeling of the House last session was unmistakably in favour of giving Captain Bernier the means that are necessary to prosecute his cherished purpose of making an expedition to the North Pole. I feel confident, from my investgations into this matter, that if Captain Bernier secures the outfit he requires, he may enter the ice pack east of Behring Straits, and that he will drift past the Pole, and will locate the Pole, and that we will in all probability have the credit of making that discovery. I think his plan is one that is calculated to secure, success. and Canada certainly could have no prouder distinction than to step in and

discover tlie North Pole after all the at-ternps that have been made by Americans, by English, by Norwegian, by Swedish navigators and others. I trust that the government will look favourably upon the application which Captain Bernier makes, and that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will urge upon his colleagues the appropriation of the necessary sum of money to carry the Captain's purpose into effect.

I presume this is not a matter which has at all any party Significance. I feel very much disposed to lend my support to the argument made by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton). From the statement made by him it would appear that Captain Bernier is contributing resources that he has accumulated by a very long and patient effort in this direction, to the extent of something like $70,000. This the Captain has collected, or has secured the promise of, by very patient, persistent devotion to a subject which is of course of very great interest. Now, it would appear that the government of Canada is asked to contribute about an equal amount; and surely if one enthusiastic citizen of Canada is prepared to contribute half the capital required, and his own services for a great many years, not only in preparation for this adventure but in carrying it. out .to a successful completion, which I hope he may succeed in doing, it is comparatively a small matter that all the other citizens of Canada collectively should contribute merely one-half of the total sum required. There can be little doubt as to the great value of the search that Captain Bernier intends to make. The discovery of the North Pole, while it may seem to a great many people to be a visionary project to which no material advantage can attach, is unquestionably one which has engaged the attention and aroused the enthusiasm of all the maritime nations of northern Europe in succession. Our cousins in the United States have made repeated efforts to discover the Pole, and I think if any people in the world should look upon it as their peculiar business, and finally succeed in making that discovery, it is the people of Canada, because the North Pole when discovered will unquestionably form part of this country. It would be an exceedingly inconvenient and unfortunate thing for us if some representative of another power should, with less advantages, beginning from a more distant point, succeed in finding the North Pole, and planting the flag possibly of some other country upon that point of the earth's surface. I think we have more reason to look upon this as particularly a Canadian object than have the people of any other nationality in the world.
There can be no doubt at all that there is a certain amount of scientific interest attached to this effort. There can be equally no doubt that it may be of great material advantage to Canada to establish finally and Mr. CHARLTON.
indisputably her claim and title to all the lands lying on the north part of this continent. Now it is possible for us at this moment to look upon this enterprise as being of no importance. It is not a long time since the whole of the north-west portion of the continent now owned by the United States, Alaska, was regarded as a country of no importance whatever. Any one looking at its position on the map would not suspect its character or importance. To-day that country is proving to be possessed of great wealth. Our own territory lying adjacent to Alaska is at this moment perhaps attracting more attention to Canada than any other part of our territory, and in this far northern region is just as likely as anywhere else to find great and valuable stores of mineral wealth. There can be no question that there are great and valuable stores of coal in those northern regions, and while they are at present inaccessible, and we have other supplies more near at hand which satisfy our requirements for the moment, we cannot tell what scientific discoveries may do in the course of a year or two. The access to that northern region, which is now almost impossible, may become, through some scientific discovery, comparatively easy, we may be able to derive from these northern portions of our possessions great wealth, great stores of mineral value. There can be of course no prospect of anything outside of minerals, but there is no reason to doubt that in those extreme northern regions,- as well as in any other portion of this northern half of the continent, may we expect to find richly mineralized lands. I know very well that Canada, while making great progress in many other directions, has depended quite as much, if not more, upon her largely increased exports of minerals for her enormously extended foreign trade, as upon any other portion of her resources. Therefore these extreme northern regions, While possessed of no agricultural value, may prove to be capable of largely expanding our exports and of adding to our national wealth. So while we may admit that national pride and scientific interest should impel us to enter at once upon an undertaking. that can be carried out at such a small cost as $80,000 or $100,000 we must recognize in addition that if we succeed through this expedition in increasing our knowledge of these regions, unpromising as they may seem at this moment vie may in the end derive benefits that will repay us tenfold or one hundred fold for any outlay we may make. I think that the enthusiasm and energy that the Captain has shown in his long continued effort to foster this child of his fancy and to carry to completion the course which he has marked out for himself and has pursued despite every kind of difficulty and doubt and disappointment, should incite us to turn with warm sympathy towards a Canadian who is willing to undergo every

discomfort and hardship that the frozen north may present, in order to accomplish the object he has set before him and should induce us to assist him in his enterprise.

I do not wish this occasion to pass without availing myself of the opportunity of expressing my hope and confidence that the government will not permit the appeal made by the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) to be lost sight of. Several years ago, when 1 first had the pleasure of hearing Captain Bernier deliver a lecture on this polar expedition and explain his views in regard to the northern hemisphere and the surroundings of the pole, I became interested in the work which he has so much at heart, and I believe that if the north pole is ever to be discovered, it will be discovered either by Captain Bernier or by some one following a course similar to that which he has marked out. He told us that he is following nature, getting nature to assist him. Instead of following the course pursued by navigators who have gone from Europe and America, he proposes to enter the ice in a different way and to follow the direction of the current which is flowing towards the pole and southward instead of going over ice which, is flowing away from the pole. In this way he has great hopes that he will discover the pole. It seems to me to be common sense reasoning that if another man has come within 200 miles of the pole and has passed it by, there should be no great difficulty in Captain Bernier coming within fifty or one hundred miles, of It, or even passing over that coveted point of the earth. It may seem something like a wild cat scheme to many in this country to talk about an expedition to the north pole ; they see no financial advantage to be gained by spending money in that way, hut to my mind the contrary is the case. Even in the matter of immigration, of making Canada known in every home in Europe, I do not believe that $100,000 could be better spent than in assisting Captain Bernier to fit out an expedition to discover the pole. Even if he fails so much would be written in the newspapers about the expedition that Canada would become a household word in every home throughout Europe, and if he succeeded in discovering the pole Canada would be known in the heart of China as well as in the heart of every European country. My suggestion is that we should provide the $100,000 which Captain Bernier requires out of the money which we have been appropriating for purposes of immigration. I believe that in that way it will accomplish a great deal more than if r. was spent on newspaper advertising or eve, in sending agents to the continent of Europe and Great Britain to solicit imm, grants to come to this country7. My object is to make Canada known, and by fitting out an expedition to the pole, whether it proves successful or not, we will
secure the aid of every newspaper in the old land in advertising Canada. That is just what we want to do ; it is by advertising Canada and making. this country known throughout Europe that we are going to get immigrants. To my mind nothing will do that more cheaply or successfully than the fitting out of such an expedition, and that is one reason why I think we should assist Captain Bernier in his very laudable purpose. The hon. member for North Norfolk has referred to another point which I think is -worthy of consideration by the government. Not long ago I saw in the newspapers that the Americans are talking very loudly of some possessions to which they propose to lay claim, away to the north of this Dominion which properly belong to the Dominion of Canada. Now, if Captain Bernier succeeds in locating the pole and planting thereon the British flag, taking possession of whatever there is in land or sea, we will certainly have a right to claim possession in the name of the King of England of everything that lies between the north pole and the now known Dominion of Canada. We will then not be troubled in the future with any Alaska boundary disputes in that direction, but will have the first claim to everything lying between what we now know as the Dominion of Canada and the North Pole. I hope the lion. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. ITefontaine), who will no doubt take an interest in this enterprise, will deeply concern himself about it, give attention to it and encourage Captain Bernier in his expedition. I hope that he will persuade the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) that the Dominion of Canada is patriotic enough and rich enough to supply the funds necessary to meet the needs of Captain Bernier's expedition. I am not at all afraid to advocate this scheme; I think it would be a great thing for the Dominion of Canada to have it said that one of her citizens was the first to plant the flag of his country upon the pole. And if the pole is ever to be discovered-and I believe it will be discovered some day-every citizen of this country would feel proud in the thought that a citizen of Canada was the first to plant the British flag upon the pole. I trust the hon. Minister of Finance will not be backward in providing a sum of money even if it is taken out of the vote which is ordinarily given for immigration purposes. I would say again : Let us devote $100,000, less to immigration and give $100,000 to Captain Bernier to fit out his expedition. If we do that I am quite sure that at the end of two or three years we will have accomplished a great deal more in the way of attracting immigrants to this country than if we had spent the sum in the ordinary way.

At the ris- of perhaps being the only member who *will speak in opposition to this project, I

desire to say a few words. I have no hesitation in saying that I am entirely opposed to the project of the Dominion of Canada granting any considerable amount for this purpose. If I am not mistaken, this is the second or third time the matter has been before the House, and1 has to certain extent received the approval of the members of this House. The attempt to discover the North Pole is a very fascinating subject, which has engaged the attention of mariners for many years. Expeditions have been fitted out in past years, and almost unlimited wealth has been expended in the attempt to discover the north pole. Nevertheless, we can safely say that the result of these expeditions has not furnished us with even sufficient information to warrant us in spending money for such a purpose. We have heard a great deal in this House recently about lack of information, but there is nothing in the world about which there is less definite information than there is about the North Pole. Those who have read the history of polar expeditions know that many lives have been sacrificed, and that wealth has been poured out lavishly without any definite result having been accomplished. It is simply a matter of sentiment, and if you should be disposed to look upon it from a commercial point of view, there is certainly no commercial advantage to be reaped. If the North Pole is ever discovered, I would be very glad indeed that it should be discovered by a Canadian, but in view of the fact that so many expeditions have failed, I have grave doubts that the North Pole will ever be found. The statement of the member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) that this expedition would be a good advertisement for Canada is to my mind rather far-fetched. When the Coldstream Guards band played here the other night, I met in the audience the gentleman who signs himself ' the wandering Yankee,' and he told me that when he first came to Canada he brought his furs along in the summer time, thinking he would require them, as he had formed his ideas of this country from the pictures sent abroad of ice palaces and winter scenes. I do not think it particularly advantageous that we should spend $100,000 to let the world know that the North Pole is in Canada. I believe we could spend $100,000 to much better advantage in advertising Canada in another direction. The hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) has told us that for 24 years Capt. Bernier has made this matter a subject of very deep concern. I would not for a moment think of detracting from the merits of Capt. Bernier. I esteem him as much as any one, and I believe that as a navigator he is entitled to much credit. But if for 24 years he has been following this visionary idea without any greater success than he has achieved, it is pretty nearlt time for him to think of something else. I believe that the House will be endn'sed

by the public at large if it once and for all sets its face against this proposition. One of the functions of government is to spend, money to the best advantage for the good of the country, but we must not think that because we have an overflowing treasury, w-e can take $100,000 from it and spend it for some impractical purpose which will bring to us no beneficial results. The hardheaded farmers of Ontario and the business people of Canada generally, would not have much sympathy for a government that has no better use for $100,000, than to spend it in chasing a chimera. For some years past they have been fitting out polar expeditions in the United States and in European countries, and I believe that the navigators of these countries are just as likely to find an easy way to the North Pole, if easy way there be, as Capt. Bernier. The simple fact that Capt. Bernier belongs to Canada, and will-start out on a new tack, does not to ray mind give an assurance whatever that be will be successful. My opinion, based upon the reports of polar expeditions in the past, convinces me that this expedition, if it be undertaken, is doomed to failure, and that the money expended for it will be absolutely thrown away.

I am very happy to support the views of the member for North Norfolk in this matter. It is very proper that the objection to this exi>edition should come from a gentleman representing a constituency in Ontario, which is the home of all the narrow ideas in Canada.
And Truro is the home of the narrow men.

For 24 years Capt. Bernier has pursued this ambition, but we know that Columbus besought. the court of Ferdinand and Isabella much longer than 24 years before he got a vessel to discover the American continent. I am not embarrassed by the statement that Capt. Bernier has besought this country for 24 years without success, but I trust that as the name of Ferdinand and Isabella are immortalized because of the aid they gave Columbus, so this country will be immortalized on account of the aid which it will give to the discoverer of the North Pole. The hon. member (Mr. Holmes) fancied that there was something derogatory to Canada in the possession of a cold but delighted climate. I am here to say that the climate of Canada is her glory. I desbe to propagate the idea that we possess a cold climate, and I shall not attempt to minimize it in the slightest degree. Any gentleman who is acquainted ivith the history of the great forces that have made, and are making this world, recognizes the benefits of a cold climate.
I desire this country to be known as a northern country. All of the [DOT] countries

of the world that have matured high civilizations have been northern countries, Germany and Russia are north of the fiftieth parallel, and they are great, dominating, world powers, while southern countries, like France, and Italy, and India, and China, are the dying nations of the world. Therefore, to be a northern country is to be a dominant and a growing country, and in that view I boast that Canada possesses the North Pole. A northern country has but one frontier to defend, and hence a northern country is most dominant in the military sense, being almost impregnable. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Holmes) peculiarly illustrates the genius of Ontario, when he says that this is a commercial question. I wonder that the people of Ontario can never rise above some little tu'penny-ha'penny consideration in the discussion of great questions. Ontario, instead of being the dominant and leading province of Canada, has almost lost her influence, because she has permitted her-i self to be influenced largely by petty commercial considerations. Gladstone and John Bright undertook to rule the British empire on those lines in Exeter Hall, and one of them had a little bit of paper, on which was figured out the cost of an insult that had been offered to England by France or the United States. Some little fellow got up and said: It will cost us five million nine hundred and twenty-six dollars and twenty-six and a half cents to avenge that insult, but, if we let the insult go and take the kicking, it will cost 36 cents less ; therefore let us take the kicking and the insult. That was the commercial argument; that is the Ontario argument. That kind of argument reduced England from a first-class power to a third or fourth-class power. Thank God, the day for that kind of argument is past, the men who made it have gone into oblivion, and we have in England to-day a dominant people who would face the world and spend every dollar they possess rather than take an insult. We have got past the commercial idea in England, and I hope we have in Canada. There are much more important ideas than the commercial idea when we are dealing with imperial questions. Sentiment rules this world, and mere figures are a secondary consideration with the great, dominant powers of the earth. Let me say one word more. Some hon. gentlemen seem to think that there is going to be a great sacrifice of life and blood in the proposed expedition. Well, what of that ? You cannot build up a nation of high civilization without the sacrifie of life and blood. That is the price any nation pays for building up a great civilization. Little Switzerland, the most civilized country in Europe, has defied the whole of Europe because it has been willing at times to sacrifice its best men and to defend its independence with its life-blood. That is the price you have to pay for high civilization and dominant political feeling. The life that would be sacrificed in this enterprise would be a noble example to the people of Canada. We want self-sacrifice. What is the good of a lazy loafer who is not prepared to make any sacrifice ? Of what value are such people to any nation ? We want men and women who are capable of selfsacrifice. The mother who tells her sou to go forth and fight for his country is the only kind of woman who is worth her salt. You want men and women who are willing to sacrifice themselves and their children, if need be, on the altar of their country. That is the only basis of high national life, and we want that sentiment in this country.
I am surprised, when the duty of selfsacrifice is mentioned, that any hon. gentleman should be averse to self-sacrifice in the direction of noble duty. The railways of the United States kill 70,000 or 80,000 people a year, and whoever hears a word of that. In the South African war when 200 or 300 people were sacrificed in a battle everybody held up their hands in horror, and said. What a terrible thing war was. But, when the trains of the United States kill that many every week, nobody says a word about it. Why, Sir, the sacrifice of life in war is the noblest way in which life can be sacrificed ; and yet you find weak writers, weak ministers, and sometimes weak members of parliament deprecating the shedding of blood. I will deprecate tire shedding of blood if it is shed for no purpose ; but if blood is shed in the best interest of the national life, there is nothing to regret. What are flesh and blood given to this world for ? At eighty years of age when life is spent, man is thrown into the earth and covered up ; is it not better at thirty or forty years of age, when life is keen and the blood is strong, to throw it away in the defence of some noble principle ? So far as I am concerned, I will support this proposal, because I do not think there is the slightest doubt about Canada owning every foot of territory from here to the North Pole. It is contiguous to Canada, and we own every foot of it by right of discovery and exploration. But if there is any doubt about it, and if we have to take physical possession of it, I am ready to support Bernier in taking physical possession of it. What we ought to do in this parliament is to husband our resources. I hear that Greenland is in the market., and if so, we ought to buy it to-morrow. Alaska was in the market a few years ago, but England did not take advantage of the opportunity to buy that country. Since then we have had enormous difficulties in consequence, and we shall continue to have difficulty in regard to Alaska until we get strong enough to ask the United States to hand over that country for a fair price to

us, as we certainly shall. If Canada succeeds in this boundary arbitration, as I hope and believe it will, the United States will still own a narrow coast line of almost 400 miles that should belong to this country. No maritime people will ever put up with a deprivation of that kind. No maritime people will ever permit a neighbouring country to own a thin strip of 400 miles of its coast; and if the United States will not sell us that territory for an equivalent sum of money, the day will come when we will take it, in spite of all the resources of the United States. It is an insult to a maritime people to be deprived of 400 miles of their coast line, and England deserves the reprobation of the Canadian people for letting Alaska go. While I am an imperialist, and while I am in love with the traditions of England and the English people, I have nothing but reprobation for the stupid diplomatists who gave away 400 miles of our coast line on the Pacific. I make a distinction between the people of England and the few men who attempt to play the role of diplomats and statesmen of England. I support Bernier's proposition, because we are the vikings of this continent. Nansen, who attempted a few years ago to reach the North Pole, was the heir of the old vikings of Norway and Sweden, who illustrated the genius of the human race on the continent of Europe ; and if the English people and the French people are great races to-day, they owe the fact to the brave old vikings, who, without compass or any of those mathematical instruments which make sea-faring safe today, went out on the turbid ocean to battle valiantly with wind and wave. No inland people can ever be a dominant people. You must have a race of men fond of the sea, battling every day with dangers to life and limb, to become a bold and dominant race. Therefore I favour this search for the North Pole. In that way we shall keep up in Canada that spirit of the vikings, the going out on unknown and sonny seas in pursuit of exploration. That makes a bold and intrepid race, which is the sort of race we want in Canada. Therefore, without figuring this matter up, according to the Toronto or Hamilton or Ontario notion of making five or ten cents profit, I support this project, because it tends to arouse and keep alive the old sentiment for life on the sea, and those feelings of high courage and enterprise that makes a noble race.

I very much fear that the country will question the sanity of this House when it finds that after sitting here for seven months we have nothing better to talk about than discovering the North Pole. On behalf of Manitoba, let me say that there are a great many things which ought to be attended to by the government as soon as possible. The St. Andrews Rapids work has been at a stand-Mr. GOURLEY.
still for upwards of a year. In Winnipeg business is almost paralyzed for the lack of room in the post office. And I am not ready to spend money on the North Pole until more immediate necessities such as this are attended to. I have been doing my best for some weeks past to get a sufficient amount of confidence in the hon. member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) to accept his curves and gradients, which he says may be obtained in that country to the north, of which he alone seems to know anything. But I cannot follow him when he goes to the North Pole and shows us exactly by what currents and curves and grades you can get there. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman ought to be content to wait and see how some of his prophecies will come out regarding our own northern country before he asks us to accept his statement about the passage of the North Pole. As to 1100,000 being spent out of the immigration grant for that purpose, that would be most absurd. We have been spending money trying to abolish the idea among Europeans that Canada is an annex of the North Pole, and our increased immigration is due to the fact that we have to a considerable extent dissipated that notion. I should therefore be opposed to our spending money in a direction which will tend to foster it.

I do not propose to detain tiie House at any length, but as this matter came under my consideration early in the session, I would like to say a few words concerning it. It was brought under my notice by a large number of members of the House of Commons and Senators, and Captain Bernier gave at that meeting a complete exposition of his plan. Last year his proposition was that we should vote him purely and simply a certain amount for the purpose of his expedition. His proposition was that we should give him from $100,000 to $120,000 to organize an expedition and carry it out. But the plan he submitted at tire meeting to which I have referred was quite different. It was one which should really commend itself to the attention of the House and the country. His proposition was that the Department of Marine and Fisheries should provide a boat, to be constructed in Canada and be loaned to him, and he would, by means of public subscriptions, get the crew and all the provisions necessary. That would entail an expenditure of about $60,000 or $70,000. Acting on that idea, Captain Bernier with commendable courage and energy succeeded in getting nearly $40,000 subscriptions. among which was a subscription of $5,000 from Lord Stratheona, and he would certainly have succeeded in getting the full amount had he been in a position to say that the Canadian government was ready to endorse his scheme. If he has succeeded in getting subscriptions to the amount of $40,-

000 without the aid of parliament, no doubt, he would with that aid, succeed in getting all the money necessary from public subscriptions. The boat to be constructed by the government would remain government property and be used for fishery protection and other purposes on the Pacific coast, provided Captain Bernier ever returned with the boat. Such a scheme should certainly commend itself to the serious attention of business men. There is not only sentiment in this matter. Of course we feel -a good deal of pride in having one of our fellow-t citizens, at Captain Bernier's age, plucky enough to undertake this perilous expedition. A great many would treat the question as just an idea without anything at the back of it. If Captain Bernier has sufficient courage to undertake this expedition at the risk of his life, that is certainly commendable even as a question of sentiment, but there is a practical side to this matter. We have organized many expeditions, most of which have been successful and given great returns. No doubt until ten years ago the territory of the Yukon was almost unknown except for two explorations made and organized by the government. Ten or fifteen years ago, if any one had stated on the floor of the House that the Yukon Territory would some day be producing from $10,000,000 to $25,000,000 of gold, people would have laughed at the idea. But how the fact has been established. The Yukon Territory to my personal knowledge-I was there a year ago-has not yet been scratched. It has not been opened really for mining in the proper sense of the word, and I have no doubt that there is an immense future for that country. Captain Bernier has held many conferences in which he has been considered a very serious man, who knew what he was talking about, and what he said about his project was taken seriously by all those who took the trouble to listen. If his proposition be simply and purely to loan a boat for the expedition, personally I do not know that there would be much objection. I understand perfectly well that this country, in developing itself so fast, requires large sums of money for things that are absolutely necessary, but that does not mean that we are going to fold our arms and let our neighbours take advantage of us. At the present time an expedition has left for the northern part of Hudson bay. And why ? Simply to organize that territory, to protect our interests in it and keep it for Canada. We have an immense territory in the direction of the North Pole, and that territory has been but little explored. It is reported, however, to be rich in minerals of all kinds. If by risking the sum of $80,000 which would be the cost of the steamer to be built for the expedition, and which could be used for something else when it returns, the exploration of that territory could be helped on, I think, personally and as a member of this House,
that the people of this country would approve of it. Of course, speaking as Minister of Marine and Fisheries, though personally quite favourable to the scheme, I must say that question has not yet been considered, because there have been so many important matters demanding the attention of the government that this question has not been specially taken up by the cabinet. But, surely if the government thinks that it should be encouraged in the way that has been suggested, I am sure that the people of the country would agree with it. And it certainly would be a credit to Canada if a Canadian should achieve the discovery of the North Pole, which nobody has been able to achieve up to the present time.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Raymond Prefontaine).

speechtext: We have been debating a region of frost and ice. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries is very anxious that assistance should be given to Captain Bernier. I desire to call his attention and that of the govern-, ment to the province of Prince Edward Island, which is not near the pole at all. That province has been deprived of the communication with the main land which the Dominion, at the time of confederation, undertook to keep up. The minister speaks in very glowing terms of the possibility of discovering the North Pole and what Captain Bernier may do in that direction. But I wish to impress upon him the fact that the government undertook with the province of Prince Edward Island to maintain communication during the winter between the Island and the mainland. Before the hon. minister undertakes to spend $80,000 or $100,000 to discover the North Pole, he should provide us with another boat to keep up this communication. The hon. gentleman says that if this boat we loan to Captain Bernier returns from the North Pole, it will be of some service. But, so far as the province of Prince Edward Island is concerned, we do not want to depend upon a boat of this kind from the North Pole. I am not opposed to this expedition. I would like to see Captain Bernier bring back enough of the North Pole to make a snuff-box. But, while I say that, I say that the government should, in the first place, carry out the terms of confederation and give to Prince Edward Island the communications that they were guaranteed at the time of confederation. And when this parliament are ready to carry out the terms of confederation in that respect, they may think about the North Pole.

Motion agreed to. and House went into Committee of Supply.
' The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding). I invite the attention of the committee again to the estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals. When we last had these estimates under consideration, two or three items were held over and

these items I now ask the committee to take up. I refer to the main estimates, page 42:
Railways and Canals-chargeable to capital- Intercolonial Railway-increased accommodation at St. John, $84,800.

I think that the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) and the kon. member for icing's (Mr. Fowler) were making inquiries about this item. I see that these lion, gentlemen are not in the House. If we could take up the Prince Edward Island items in the meantime, these kon. gentlemen might be with us later on.

I do not think that there is anything that tile lion, gentlemen would object to in this item. I shall be glad to give any information asked for, and, if the items are adopted, that shall (not shut off discussion. With regard to this item for St. John, I may explain that we had an appropriation for this service last year of $90,500. That amount was expended, and a little more, including the purchase of some land under a judgment given by the Exchequer Court. The actual expenditure was $3,000 odd in excess of the appropriation. We ask here for an appropriation of $106,000, of which a one-fifth has already been voted. We shalll ask in the sup-plementaries to lie brought down a further sum of $5,000. So we shall have for expenditure on the works at St. John $111,000. I gave the details of this on a previous occasion, but I may summarize them now. The sum of $41,355.50 is to pay the balance of the contract for the engine house and machine shop; $10,000 for coal shed ; $10,000 for boilers and engines, and $10,000 for grading and track laying, and various small items.
Are these manufacturing shops ?
The engine house and machine shop are for repairs. The manufacturing is done at Moncton.
Is it anticipated that there will be a greatly increased trade by adopting St. John as a winter iiort ? And is that why we need to make this heavy expenditure ?

The larger portion of the winter port business is done by the Canadian Pacific Railway on the other side of the harbour. But the general business of ,St. John has grown very much, and it is necessary to make these improvements for its accommodation. The work is now in progress, the contract having been let for the engine house and machine shop.

But, if the Canadian Pacific Railway is doing the major portion of the work and the Intercolonial is not, what justification can there be for this Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
greatly increased expenditure ? Is the business of the Intercolonial Railway increasing rapidly in St. John of late ?

In what I said regarding the Canadian Pacific Railway doing business, I did not imply that the Intercolonial is not doing any, but the Canadian Pacific Railway is doing a winter port business, Which is handled on the western side of the harbour. But the general business and trade at St. John are decidedly increasing, and we desire to increase the facilities for handling that business. An engine-house is also rendered necessary by the fact that we are now using engines of much larger size, and we require larger engine-houses. The modern engines cannot get into the old engine-house.
A few years ago we were told that the roadbed was in first-class condition, and afterwards) it turned out when the new engines were purchased that it was dangerous to take them over the bridges.

The hon. gentleman knows that there has been quite a development in railroading. You have to build larger engines, heavier cars ; and the equipment of railways is different from what it was a few years ago.

It was contended on this side of the House that the road was not suitable for the heavier rolling stock, and unless it was made more substantial this rolling stock could not be used to advantage. Now, with regard to the engine-house, if you require to expend over $100,000 in one place for an engine-house, it seems you must either be expecting greatly increased trade there in future, or else your old engine-house must have been very inferior in the first place.
The old engine-house was part of the original construction of the road, and was built before confederation, and naturally was not adapted to the conditions which exist at present.
Could the minister tell us what quantity of winter freight is being carried, and whether much grain is carried to St. John in the winter ?

A very small quantity of grain passed through the elevator, but the general business of the Intercolonial is increasing at St. John.
Increased accommodation at Halifax, $83,600.

We had a considerable appropriation for Halifax last year, but a large amount of it was not expended, and we have to revote it now, with some additional sums. The appropriation last year was $143,000, of which we expended $75,174. So there is a balance of last years's expenditure to de carried forward, in the form of a revote, of $67,826.

The revote here is stated to be $104,500. That estimate was made some months ago, and is now found not to be correct. We are taking in this item an additional sum of $36,674, making the sum of $104,500 which is accounted for in the main estimates. We have, however, other works on hand in Halifax which we shall have to provide for in the supplementary estimates, and which will make the total appropriation for the year, including these revotes of last year, $229,500. The details of this sum are : Land for engine-house and yard, $20,000 ; laud at Cornwallis street, $20,000 ; grading and other work in connection with the proposed engine house, $20,000 ; to complete improvements at station, $7,500 ; construction of quay wall of crib-work, $37,000 ; wharfs and freight shed, $125,000. A part of the sum wie are asking will be included in the supplementary estimates. With regard to the land for the engine house, we have not yet determined on the location, and we shall be obliged probably to go outside of the city limits, where we have some land in our mind's eye. It is not wise at present to state where it is. We have, of course, in view two or three different locations, and we think we shall be able to acquire the land at a moderate cost. We wish also to acquire a small amount of land south of the elevator at Halifax, partly because it is likely to be applied to other purposes if we do not purchase it, and also because we shall need it if we are to do any business at all with the elevator, to allow tracks to run through the elevator, so that the cars may pass through and go off on another track. At present there is not a great deal of that kind of business done at Halifax nor at St. John. But for any business that may be done at the elevator, the cars at present have to go in and then back out again, which makes considerable delay. It is desirable that we should purchase a small quantity of land on the other side of the elevator so that, tracks may be laid down on which the cars may pass through the elevator, while others come up behind. These, together with wharf improvements, are the changes and operations which we propose to carry on.
After this new transcontinental road is built, do you expect to need all this heavy expenditure to accommodate the trade that you are likely to get over the Intercolonial at Halifax and St. John ?

Well, I differ with my hon. friend on that point ; but to my mind, after building this railway, there will be more business at St. John and Halifax than there is now. The Intercolonial buildings will all be required, and probably more. However, even without the transcontinental railway, we require this accommodation at Halifax :	and we also
require, apart from the elevator, which will
only be used for the grain traffic-but leaving that out of the question, for the business of the Intercolonial we undoubtedly need the greater accommodation in land and buildings, both at St. John and Halifax.

I do not object to the expenditure if it is needed. But it does seem a little suspicious. We expended a large sum for an elevator at St. John some time ago for the purpose of handling grain on the Intercolonial, but we have never had any grain to handle. That was not a wise expenditure. To-day you propose to purchase more land to run cars through the elevator, but there is no grain to handle, and according to the outlook you are not likely to have any grain to handle in the future. It seems to me to be providing accommodation for a trade which we have not yet got, and that the money expended in it will not be earning any interest. I do not think that is wise ; in fact, it is very unwise, but if there is clearly indication that the trade requires it, I for one do not feel like Objecting to the expenditure. .

I think that if we should take the position that we should first get the trade and then build the elevator, instead of building the elevator so as to be prepared to handle the trade, we would be reasonably and justly open to criticism and to be asked : How can you expect trade when you provide no facilities ? As to additional land to be purchased near the elevator at Halifax, for which $20,000 is asked, I may say that this land is close by the deep water terminus in the centre of the north part of the city. We had some reason to believe that this property was about to be purchased and a costly build-i ing to be placed upon it. Then, if in a short time we should require that ground, we would have to buy it with the buildings added, and we thought that as the buildings now on it are of a very poor character, we should buy it now. It was thought wise by the railway authorities to purchase the land. We have not yet purchased it, because the parties who own it are not willing to accept the price we offer, and we may be obliged! to go into the Exchequer Court.	We-have made an offer which they
do not wish to accept. I may say that in these purchases .of property we do not wish to go into the Exchequer Court, because it is an expensive proceeding.
What portion of these works are now under contract or under con-* struction ?	.

There is some costly work to be done on one of the old wharfs, and it is proposed to build some new wharfs further north. It is proposed) also to buy some land outside the city to put up an engine-house. I think that only a small amount of work has yet been under-

taken; in fact, it is a subject of criticism that they have not done more with it.
Is it intended to do these works and to put up these buildings by tender, or does the government propose to do the work by any other means ?

Works of this character are usually done by tender.
Mr. SPItOULE. I think the minister has an idea whether he will or will not do this work by tender, and his answer appears to me to be an evasive answer.

It was not intended to be an evasive one ; I have no intention of doing it otherwise than by tender, but at the same time if any reason should arise why, in my judgment, or in the judgment of the government, it appears better that it should be done otherwise, I would wish to be free.
Have tenders been asked for any part of it yet ?

For the Halifax work tenders have been asked for creosoted piles for one of the wharfs ; that is the only work that has yet been started. Owing to the difficulty of obtaining the land the work has been delayed.
Increased accommodation at Pictou, $29,200.

We had an appropriation last year for this work of $70,000, and the work in that case also, owing to some difficulty in obtaining the land has been delayed, and we have not been able to make as much progress as we expected. The actual expenditure out of that vote has been $12,155.10, so that the unexpended balance at the close of the year which is to be revoted, is $57,884,490. This sum of $57,884, carried over from last year with $40,355, which we shall have to add, makes a total of $98,200, which Is the amount that we expect to be authorized to expend in Pictou this year. Of this we are taking $30,500 in the main estimates, and we shall have to ask in the supplementary estimates for the balance of $61,700. This $98,200 is made up as follows : Land, $27,000 ; piles and trestles, $10,000; new station, $30,000. There are also various smaller Items, making up the total of $98,200. Pictou is the point at which a large part of the business with Prince Edward Island is carried on ; the station buildings are somewhat old and we are desirous of making considerable improvements. We have selected some land, but it has not yet been purchased, because the price asked is higher than we feel disposed to give, but we are now negotiating and hope to obtain the property at a lower price.
Improvements at Little Metis station and diverting public road, $3,200.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
When this item was before the committee the other night, I was asked to explain what portion of it went for land and what for the road, and other improvements. I find now that the estimated cost of the land is $300 and the cost of building the road $1,200, making $1,500. Then, there are the expenses of moving the station and tank and enlarging the station, which is estimated at $2,500. These items together make the $4,000 for which the vote is asked. Little Metis is the principal summer resort on the Intercolonial Railway, and is visited by a large number of people from various parts of the Dominion, particularly from Montreal and vicinity, and this improvement seems to be very necessary.
Prince Edward Island-to widen wharf and to provide coal sheds at Summerside, $1,600.

It is proposed by this expenditure to increase the size of the coal shed so as to afford more shed room on the wharf. We made some expenditure last year upon the other side of the wharf, but this further expenditure is deemed necessary, especially for the accommodation of the coal trade.

Summerside railway wharf is the only place where goods can be landed for transit throughout the Island, and there is only one side of the wharf at which a vessel can get accommodation. At a meeting of the maritime board of trade held recently this question was considered and the following resolution adopted :
That better facilities should be provided at the railway wharf at Summerside to accommodate the steamers landing freight for transportation over the Prince Edward Island Railway.
Most of the freight coming through Prince Edward Island from the west, is brought to Summerside, and it has to be stored in the warehouse before being shipped. There is also a very extensive shipment of goods from different points on the Island to the railway wharf. Increased accommodation is badly needed there. Only one steamer can lie at that wharf, and other steamers have to land their freight at private wharfs, so that the goods have to be trucked across the town at increased cost. I trust that both the wharf and warehouse accommodation will be improved there. I have seen the warehouse so overcrowded, that flour and other merchandise had to remain outside.
The improvements contemplated by this vote will I am sure be appreciated so far as they go. I shall give careful consideration to the representations made by the hon. gentleman.

This work contemplates an improvement to the coal slied, and that is all right so far as it goes, but the other improvements are of great necessity.

Murray Harbour branch and Hillsborough bridge, $600,000.

This is a large item, but as lion, gentlemen know, we have undertaken quite a costly work in the extension of the railway from Charlottetown to Murray harbour, inasmuch as a very expensive bridge has to be provided for. In the main estimates we ask for $750,000, a portion of which has already been voted, and we are asking the balance now. In the supplementary estimates we shall have to ask a further sum of $480,000, so that the expenditure which we expect to make on that work during the current year, including the bridge, will be $1,230,000. There was expended on this work up to the 30th June, $1,492,525.47, so that if we take the expenditure to the 30th of June, and the amount we shall have to ask for the current year, these sums make the cost of the work, as estimated up to the end of the current year, $2,795,113.19. The road is already constructed as far as Murray river, and it will take six miles more to carry it down to Murray harbour, which extension is included in the estimate which I have given for the year, and which will have to bo provided for in the supplementary estimates. There is also a wharf to be built at Murray harbour, where navigation is open four weeks earlier in the spring and four weeks later in the fall than at Murray river. AVe propose to carry the road down, as the Act contemplated, from Charlottetown to Murray harbour. The total expenditure for the whole work completed will be about $3,-000,000 in round numbers. The bridge is a very costly bridge.
What is the tender for the bridge ?
The tender is on schedule prices, and the estimated cost of the bridge is $1,494,097.
Is the estimated cost likely to be increased or decreased 7

I do not think there will be any change which would increase the cost of the bridge. It was known from the beginning that it would be a very expensive undertaking. I may say in reply to a question put to me some time ago, that there is a contract between the Dominion and local governments, by which the local government is to contribute to the Dominion the sum of $9,750 per annum for this bridge, and the local government reserves the right to levy tolls on the highway portion of it, if they should see fit to do so.
For how long are they to pay that ?
It is a permanent charge which is to be deducted from their subsidy, or any payment that may be due them.
