speechtext: On what basis is the schedule of prices for the building of the bridge arranged 7
It is the usual method of taking tenders for a work of that character.
I thought you said you could not give the exact cost of the bridge, because it was based on schedule prices ?
There is a lump sum for the superstructure, and the schedule price applies to the masonry, &c.
How much has been expended on the bridge up to the present time ?
The expenditure on the substructure and approaches up to the 30th June, 1903, is $733,101.99.

I understand that the work on the bridge lias not been proceeded with as rapidly as the government promised and that the contractor lias been very little on the ground, pushing the work, this year. When does the minister expect that the bridge will be finished and open for traffic V

The work, like most large undertakings of the kind, has not gone on as rapidly as we might desire. The probable date of the completion of the substructure of the bridge is fixed at the 31st of December of this year, and the probable date of the completion of the superstructure at the 30th of June, 1904.
You say the railway has been completed from Charlottetown to Murray river. How many miles would that be 7	'
Forty-four miles to Murray river, and G1 miles further to Murray harbour, making 501 miles for the whole length.
AAras this 44 miles tendered for ?

Yes, in the first instance ; it was awarded to a party who did not take it. It was then passed to the next tenderer. At a later stage the subsequent portion of the work was given to that contractor at the same rate as the tender price.
Who was the contractor ?
Mr. Willard Kitchen.
Is he the contractor for the bridge 7
No; the contractor for the bridge is Mr. M. J. Haney.

The 61 miles of railway was not contemplated at the time the contract for the 44 miles was let 7

[DOT] 12832
No. The contract was let only to Murray river, and we propose to build the railway to Murray harbour.

Has the contract for the 6J miles been let ?
of the railroad, people who have some little idea of the construction of railroads, and they report that the culverts along the line from Charlottetown to Murray river are not fit to be under any railroad or tramroad, as they are not properly constructed.
No.
Is it proposed to let it by tender V
We have not given that any consideration. We have no intention to build it otherwise than by public tender; but if there are good reasons why we should not do that, I would like to hold myself free.
What is the estimate for the wharf at Murray harbour ?

The estimate is much larg<A' than I thought it should be, and I have been asking the engineers if it can be reduced. I have included in these figures an estimate for crib-work, which is to cost something over $00,000. It is a question whether we can reduce this figure. The place is very much exposed, and we may have to build a wharf there of a very substantial character, and the estimate for that is, I think, $09,000.
Do you charge the building of that wharf to the capital account of the Intercolonial Railway ?
Yes.
Is there any distinction between building that wharf and building wharfs all over the county and charging them to harbours and rivers ?
Wharfs built as part of the terminal facilities of the Intercolonial Railway are all considered to be part of the railway, and are charged to capital.
What is the cost of this railway per mile ?
It is difficult to make an estimate of the cost of the railway per mile without the bridge. I do not think we have the figures in that form.
Is there any standard to which this road has to be built ? Is it to be built as well as the Grand Trunk Railway between Montreal and Toronto, apart from the double track ?

No. I think it will be as good as the railway from Charlottetown to Murray river. We like to have standards which the people can see. When the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, the standard fixed was some railway in the United States that the people of Canada knew nothing about. We want a standard which the people can see.
I have had several communications from people in the locality Mr. LEFURGEY. *

I am bound to take notice of what my hon. friend says, but I can only say that no such representations have reached me. Of course, the island railway is a narrow gauge road, and does not require to be built according to the standard of a larger road. But we do want good and substantial work ; that is what we are paying for, and if we are not getting it, there is something wrong. But the work is constructed under competent engineers, and I cannot think that they would accept work of the character my hon. friend describes.
Why would it not be easy to arrive at a calculation of the cost of the railway per mile apart from the bridge ?

I did not say it would be difficult to arrive at it. I said I did not happen to have the figures before me. The deputy minister informs me that it cost $21,500 per mile without the bridge.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) I was somewhat surprised at the statement made by my hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey), to the effect that the character of the road was so poor. My information is just the opposite.
1 did not say the general character of the road. I said the culverts.

That is a part of the road and a very important part. It is very strange that if that is the case I have not heard anything about it. I live pretty near that part of the country. If the railway does not run through the district I represent, it runs close to it. As a matter of fact, I have been speaking to some railway men, who belong to the Prince Edward Island Railway and who would have no interest in misrepresenting the matter in any way.

You do not suppose I would.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) No. But I do not know the men who gave my hon. friend the information. I do not mean to say for one moment that he would misrepresent ; but possibly the matter may have been misrepresented to him. The men I have been speaking to ou the subject are practical railway men, and they have told me that it is an excellent road, a much better one than the older part of the Prince Edward Island Railway was when it was built.
Were they contractors?
No, and they have no interest whatever in the contractors. They are Prince Edward Islanders, who would be interested in having a good road.
Are they brakesmen ?
No ; they are men who have been engaged in the construction of railways.
Then they have been contractors ?
No, they have been employed with contractors in railway work. They have no interest at all in Mr. Kitchen's contract, not the slightest, no more than my hon. friend.

The information came to me in several communications, and I have given it to you as I got it. I only call the attention of the minister to it in order that it may be looked into. I would like to know how this amount of $9,750 which the provincial government is to pay has been arrived at ?

I am afraid I can hardly answer that question. It was originally fixed at a larger sum, in the earlier negotiations. The estimate for the bridge was less than was thought in the first negotiations, and this sum was fixed by Act of parliament in the year 1901 confirming the arrangement made with the government of Prince Edward Island,
What are we to understand by a narrow gauge road ?
The railway on the island is not the standard gauge, but three feet six.
What is the lay of this country ? I always understood that it was level.
It is not level, but there are no very high mountains. It is a rolling country.

I am satisfied with the plan of the hon. minister with regard to the substructure of the bridge. But how will the superstructure be carried on ? Are we to have some of the old bridges on the Intercolonial taken across and placed as a superstructure on that work ? The people of the island, according to the statement of the hon. gentleman, are paying $9,750 per year for this accommodation.

Mr. Haney's contract is for the substructure, $1,218,000. The superstructure represents $275,000. We are not to have any played-out bridges, but some good, strong bridges, suitable for the island, are to be taken from the Intercolonial.
From what part of the Intercolonial are those bridges coming ?
From the Miramiehi river.
The south-west or northwest branches ?	.
The chief engineer thinks south-west, but not very positive.
What is their age ?
They were built in 1872.
Did not the hon. min-' ister a few days ago give a bridge of the same age to be used as a traffic bridge between Quebec and the province of New Brunswick, without charging anything at all for it ?
We are not charging this to the island.

Yes, you are compelling the province to pay $9,750 per year for this superstructure, where there shall be a carriage way alongside, and I think that it is strange that a present should be made to the rich province of Quebec and the province of New Brunswick, while you insist upon Prince Edward Island paying the last farthing.

I think, in view of those large figures, that my hon. friend will hardly get a great deal of sympathy when he complains that the island is badly treated. Over the Restigouche there was a bridge for which we had no use. If we could have used it on any other part of the government system, we would have done so, but there was no place for which it was adapted, so that it was practically worthless. We offer it to the provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec as our contribution for an iron bridge between the two provinces, but the municipalities or the provinces will have to provide considerable expenditure in the making of that bridge. We occasionally grant . sums for interprovincial bridges, and we deal with new Brunswick and Quebec as we deal with other provinces between which there are interprovincial bridges.

I am not objecting at all to what is being done at Restigouche, but I object that, while the provinces of New Brunswick and Quebec are dealt with in one way, Prince Edward Island is dealt with differently. What doles the acting minister intend doing in connection with the building of a railway station at Charlottetown ? That has been in discussion for many years, and the present railway station is not at all fitted for its purpose. Does the hon. minister intend now to build a proper railway station in Charlottetown ?
We expect to provide for some improvements in Charlottetown in the supplementaries.
What is the cost per mile of that road ?
$21,500 per mile. It is a narrow gauge road through a hilly country, with a considerable amount of rock.
If the bridge cost a million and a half and the whole expenditure was $2,795,000, the railway, being 45 miles in length, must have cost $28,000 a mile.
That would include the bridge.
No.
It is 50i miles over the whole line-44 miles to Murray river and 6J miles from Murray river to Murray harbour.
That would make it about $28,000 a mile.
I would like to ask the acting Minister of Railways and Canals if he has had any communication from any source, inside or outside this House, with regard to a line to Elmira ?

I have had communication verbally and, I think, in writing-at any rate, I know that a desire has been expressed for one or two extensions. But I do not remember the name of Elmira. Perhaps the bon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey) has better information than I have.

Among the lines very much needed in Prince Edward Island is one to Elmira. I think my hon. friend from King's (Mr. Hughes) will explain that point somewhat fully. I have here a resolution passed by a public meeting held on the 27th, of February, at which speeches were made by Messrs. John McLean, M. L. A., J. J. Hughes, M.P., and others. And the following resolution was passed :	.
Whereas a survey for a branch line of railway was made in the year 1882 by the then government of Canada ; and whereas
The government of 1895 promised to construct several branch railways on Prince Edward Island, among which was the Elmira branch ; and
Whereas a delegation from Elmira had a promise from Sir L. H. Davies when Minister of Marine and Fisheries that upon the completion of the Murray Harbour Railway he would use his influence with the Minister of Railways to cause a survey to be made and estimates prepared and submitted to parliament for the construction of a branch line to Elmira ; and whereas
Since that time largely increased expenditures for railways and other public works have been made in nearly every part of the Dominion ;
Therefore resolved that the residents of East Point and vicinity, in meeting assembled, Mr. HACKETT.
strongly urge upon the government the necessity of commencing this important work at an early date, and also request our representatives in parliament to press this matter upon the Minister of Railways during the coming session.
It seems to me very strange that the acting Minister of Railways and Canals had not heard fully of this branch line to Elmira, seeing that the hon. member for King's was one of the prominent speakers on this occasion. But if the hon. gentleman has not spoken of it, I wish it to be borne in on the hon. minister on this occasion that there are other places in Prince Edward Island that need railway facilities; and, while I do not know so much about this railway to Elmira, I have on several occasions brought to the notice of the government the promise that was made to the people of Prince Edward Island that a brunch line was to be constructed from North Wiltshire to Crapaud. On two occasions, I think, petitions were presented to this House largely signed, by persons irrespective of politics, for branch lines through that thriving settlement. It would run through a country from 15 to 20 miles away from railway communications, and would be of great service to the people there. There are also several much shorter lines in the western part of the province to which, I think, the attention of the government has been called on several occasions. I think we have the right to expect some promise or some indication of wbat the government's intentions are as to these branch lines.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) My hon. friend from East Prince (Mr. Lefurgey), speaking of the branch line to Elmira, said he did not know much about it I am quite convinced of that fact. He does not know much about it, or he would not have mentioned it. I did not intend to make any remarks about this matter, and would not but for the ill-advised statements of the member for East Prince. I should be sorry to refer to any matters in the hon. gentleman's district while he is a member of the House and present. I take it that he is quite able to take care of his own district, and I think that I am able tol take care of the part of Prince Edward Island which I represent. The facts are, that while the hon. gentleman's friends were in power a survey was made from Harmony, near Souris, to Elmira, just on the eve of an election. But when the election was over nothing further was done. And so the people were deceived. In fact, they were deceived twice by running a survey over that part of the country. After the first survey the stakes were allowed to rot, and when the next survey was made they were not to be found. As a supporter of the government, I would not ask the government to do anything of that kind. Tlie hon. gentleman has referred to a meeting

at Elmira, or rather at Lakeville, near Elmira. If he has a true report of that meeting, he will find that I stated that, until the road to Murray harbour was completed,
I would not take this matter up, as I thought the government was doing fairly well for Prince Edward Island in the matter of building railways. And I think so still. I ha#e told the people that I would not bring this up as an election dodge, nor would I bring it up until the Murray harbour road was completed. But, when that road is built, I shall bring this to the attention of the government upon its merits as a fair and reasonable commercial proposition. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Lefurgey) was ill-advised when he brought this matter up. I did not intend to refer to these old subjects, but I could not avoid it in view of the fact that his party, when in power, deliberately twice deceived the people of the eastern part of King's county, in the hope of affecting an election. I would not ask the government to do anything of that kind, and if I did ask them, I do not think they would consent.

I am sorry the hon. member for King's (Mr. Hughes) got so excited over this matter.
Mr. HUGHES (King's, P.E.I.) I am not excited, but I have stated some facts that are not palatable to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lefurgey).

I have brought this matter up on several occasions, and intend1 to bring it up again until I get some satisfaction as to the intentions of the government with regard to these lines. The hon. member (Mr. Hughes, King's) may be very well satisfied with the work going on in the eastern part of the province, where they are getting fifty miles of railway built, while the people of the western section have none. He may well be quiet for a year or two. I have simply taken occasion to remind the government of a promise made by Sir Louis Davies that on the completion of the road now under construction, the road to Elmira would be looked after. But merely because one road is under construction, is that any reason why the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, King's) should not press his claims on the government. Is he too bashful ? Well, I can tell him that, while I am in this House I consider myself as a representative not only of my own district, but of his district as well, which is in an integral part of the Dominion, and I am a representative of the Dominion. I do not intend to keep quiet, even though the hon. gentleman does get excited; and if he does not see St to ask for more railway communication for the eastern part of the island, I shall do so myself.

Can the minister say that a new station will be built in Charlottetown within a year ?
402$
I will ask my hon. friend to be patient, because the supplementary estimates will be down to morrow. I cannot promise that they will satisfy him absolutely, but they will be encouraging.

There is another matter I desire to call to the attention of the minister, and that is the construction of a new station at Alberton, in the county of West Prince. The station there is really an old ramshackle, one of the first erected on the Island, over thirty years ago.
Leave something for Ontario.
You are asking us to vote away over $100,000,000 for building a railway from Moncton to Winnipeg.
Do you have to pay for it ?

We have to pay our proportion of it, and we insist upon receiving our share of the public moneys of the Dominion of Canada. Now might I ask the minister again if he intends to build this station at Alberton, in the county of West Prince, within a short time ?
I think my hon. friend will have to have some faith and not cross examine us too closely. I will not say ' wait till you see us next year,' but wait till you see the supplemen-taries.

There is another matter I desire to bring to the attention of the minister, and that is the building of a branch line of railway from O'Leary Station to the west shore of Prince Edward Island. There have been petitions sent asking for it, and many meetings held advocating it. The people are desirous of having this branch line constructed. While my hon. friend from West York (Mr. Campbell) appears to be very indignant because we insist upon having our rights in the expenditure of public money, he is quite willing to vote away a hundred million dollars of the public money, while he would not give us a hundred thousand dollars in the province of Prince Edward Island to complete out-railway system. I hope the minister will see his way clear to do something in connection with a branch from O'Leary to the west shore of Prince Edward Island.

I am sorry to hear that my hon. friend from West York is not willing to give Prince Edward Island a hundred thousand dollars, because I am asking my hon. friend from West York to vote $1,230,000 for Prince Edward Island in this one item alone.

How many tenders did you receive for the substructure of this bridge, and who was the lowest tenderer V

12S40

This contract was let to Mr. Haney on the 25th of August, 1900. We expect the bridge will be finished at the end of the calendar year, and we hope the whole work will be finished by the 30th of June, 1904.
Mr. SPItOULE. Will the minister bring down the information regarding this contract, the parties tendering and the amount of each tender ?
Is tills superstructure to cost $275,000 over and above the bridges that are taken off the Intercolonial Railway ?
No, a value will be put upon the bridges and credited to the Intercolonial account. The $275,000 will include the price which will be paid to the Intercolonial and also the cost of erection.

The minister brushed aside the remarks I made very easily. But he must remember this first, that while we are voting this large amount for the construction of this bridge, the government and people of Prince Edward Island are bound to pay $9,750 in interest upon that sum. Now if you are voting a million dollars or so, you are obliging the people to contribute that much. I shall make no apology for bringing up the matter in this House.

With regard to the people of Prince Edward Island paying this sum of money, I do not wish the hon. gentleman to offer an apology, but unintentionally he has omitted an important fact. This bridge is being constructed for two purposes, partly for a railway bridge and partly for a highway bridge. The Dominion of Canada is paying every copper of the cost so far as it relates to the railway, and the local government are contributing a share towards the bridge in consideration of the fact that it provides a highway for them, and It is their business to provide a highway.
What valuation do you put on these bridges that are taken from over the Miramichi river ?

The value placed on the bridges for the purpose of being credited in the Intercolonial Railway accounts is $64,000. The remaining portion of the value placed on the bridges represents the cost of transportation and erection.
Will the bridges be sufficient to cover the distance between Southport and Charlottetown ?
Yes, the bridges will be quite sufficient for the purpose.
In addition to that you have to. provide the carriage way by the side of the bridge ?

That is included in the figures I gave.
Increased accommodation at Kensington, $500.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE, One-fifth of this has already been voted.

This is for increased accommodation at Kensington. I have a letter from one of the chief business men in Kensington in regard to these improvements and for the benefit of the acting Minister of Railways and Canals I wish to read this in order to give him an idea of what is required there. He says :
A memorial asking for a new station building here was sent to Mr. Blair a few days ago from the committee appointed at a meeting of the patrons of the station here held on October last. And since then we see that $1,000 is in the estimates for repairs of the old one presumably by Mr. Sharpe's plan. Now, ow ng to increased business, both freight and passenger lately, and especially as it is here the summer tourists for Malpeque and New London take and leave the train, decent and if possible attractive accommodation should be had. At present it is the very reverse. The change proposed by Mr. Sharpe would be very little better, whilst it would stand in the way of getting a new building for some time. For instance, he proposed taking a portion of the old freight-shed (ceiling 8 feet 6 inches), under a flat roof and saturated with oil, petroleum and other things and converting it into a ladies' waiting room, and all his other changes according to that. We had some differences with Mr. Sharpe and now he is getting square with us. He could not say but the old building as you know, with only one waiting-room, where every class of persons have to wait for hours at night waiting for belated trains as is very common, yes, from, wealthy, refined Americans and other tourists down to Indians and drunken toughs, is not fit for use. But he wants to patch it up in any shape and punish the public for the criticism offered to him about the present state of affairs.
Now, this section is one of the principal shipping points between Charlottetown and Summerside, possibly the largest town between these two points, and it is a place of considerable commercial importance, as the writer slates here it is a point where a great many tourists coming to Prince Edward Island leave and take the trains to go to the watering places and they have had but tlie one station where Indians, ladies and all congregate to wait for trains which at this point are necessarily late leaving Summerside and arriving through from Charlottetown. When $1,000 is being spent to make repairs in this station it seems to me that at a point so central as this the government might very well spend a little more, a thousand or two, whatever is necessary and build a suitable station. I merely 1 want to call the attention of the minister to

this before any expenditure is made upon it in order that he may have an opportunity to investigate. I wish also to say that their freight accommodation and the plut-form arrangements for passengers are very deficient and require some attention. Before sitting down I would also wish to put in a word for the improvements at Charlottetown and to say that I am entirely in accord with what Mr. Haekett said that the station is an old and dilapidated affair and the people there certainly need a new station. They also need increased accommodation along their water-front for the different private wharfs. There is no way of- getting at the freight in these places unless you cart it straight across the town to Charlottetown station.
To improve the water service, $19,200.

At present they use wells on the Prince Edward Island Railway, and we propose to place upon the system a modern method of supplying the railway with water from tanks.
To provide additional accommodation at Kin-kora, $640.

Is it intended to make this a booking station ? Unless it is made a booking station the residents of that section of the country extending from Emerald and Albany to Kinkora, will not be able to [DOT] get their goods without sending their money to Emerald. Trains pass this station late at night and early in the morning, and the booking station is an absolute necessity.

We propose to erect a building forty feet by twenty feet, in which there will be a waiting room and baggage room. The business at the station is not very great, and I think probably it will have to be a flag station for the present.
The business of the station cannot be great when you do not afford accommodation.
At all events this is a step in the right direction.

ICinkora is a very prominent point on the line from Emerald to Cape Traverse, and I would urge the minister to have a regular booking station and telegraph office there.
New stations at Northam and Richmond, $800.
Will these buildings be erected before the winter V
We will try. I cannot promise.
Will these stations be similar to the stations at Elmsdale and Conway, and have a fire and caretaker, without being regular booking stations ?
The station will be similar to that at Kinkora.
We have now passed the railway estimates, and as it is after twelve o'clock, we should adjourn.

I think the request is reasonable.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What business will be taken up to-morrow ?

The orders are so reduced in number now, that it is very easy to make a selection. We might take up some Bills which have already been discussed, and we will perhaps go on with supply. That is as definite as I can state at present. If we go on with supply we will proceed from the point at which we left off.
Motion agreed to, and the House adjourned at 12.25 a.m. Thursday.
